problems.title: Opportunity Navigator
problems.summary: Jobs, courses and scholarships exist on dozens of sites. Put them where a young person can use them.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Dream a Dream is a Bengaluru non-profit that works with children and young people from vulnerable backgrounds. Its method is life skills and social-emotional learning, not academic coaching. It runs Thriving Centres for young people, works inside government schools, and has state hubs across India. It points out that 54% of India’s young people are not ready for work.
detail.situation: A young person at a Thriving Centre wants a job, a course, or money to study. The information they need already exists. It is spread across dozens of websites, in more than one language, written for people who already understand the system. Government schemes for education, jobs, skills, business and financial support sit on separate central and state portals, each with its own rules and forms.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Young people find opportunities through people they already know. Their networks are small, so their options are small. Someone with an uncle in a bank hears about bank jobs. Someone without one hears about nothing.

Dream a Dream describes the failure as a sentence: young people can say “I am interested in this” but cannot say “I know what I can do next”. Interest does not turn into a step.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Job portals exist and are useless here. They assume a degree, a resume, a stable internet connection, and enough English to read a listing. They rank by employer need, not by what a young person could realistically get. Scholarship aggregators go stale within a year because the deadlines move and nobody maintains them.

The hard part is not collecting listings. It is judging which of them a specific person can actually get, and saying so honestly.
detail.whatExists:
Dream a Dream runs a career awareness approach today, and asks you to go beyond it rather than repeat it.

Ask them what that approach covers, what tools the facilitators use, and what has already been tried and dropped. Do that before you design anything.
detail.whatYouHave:
- public government scheme portals and their data, where it is published
- access to Thriving Centre facilitators and young people for interviews, subject to Dream a Dream’s consent process
- any opportunity list, spreadsheet or partner feed Dream a Dream already keeps — ask whether it can be shared
detail.doneIn90Days: A working tool that a facilitator can sit down with a young person and use. It has to do three things: find opportunities the young person would not have found alone, say plainly whether they are eligible and what it would take, and end with a next step specific enough to act on this week. It must work for someone reading in Kannada as comfortably as in English, and on a low-end Android phone.
detail.rules:
- no scraped personal data about young people leaves Dream a Dream’s control
- the tool must not invent an opportunity, a deadline or an eligibility rule — if you cannot source it, say so on screen
- it must be usable by a facilitator with no technical training, on a phone, offline for at least the reading parts
detail.findingYourApproach:
Your first idea will probably be everyone else’s. Before you commit to it, find out what already exists in this space and why none of it has solved the problem for a young person at a Thriving Centre.

Then answer the questions a good approach has to answer: who keeps this accurate in month seven, how do you prove an eligibility claim is right, and what does the tool do when the honest answer is that this person is not eligible for anything yet?
detail.sponsor:
Dream a Dream.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT. Some room for design-minded students from any branch.
- **Technical skills** — Data collection and cleaning, search and ranking, retrieval over documents, multilingual interfaces, low-bandwidth front-end work.
- **Other skills** — User interviews, writing plainly for a reader who is not you, judging a source’s reliability.

problems.title: Community Asset and Youth Mapping
problems.summary: Map the young people, employers and services within 8 to 10 km of a centre.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Dream a Dream, as described in Brief 01. This problem sits with the team that runs the Thriving Centres and decides who the centre should be reaching.
detail.situation: A Thriving Centre sits in a neighbourhood. Within 8 to 10 kilometres of it there are young people who have left school, young people about to leave, employers, training institutes, clinics, libraries, sports grounds, self-help groups and small businesses. Some of that is recorded in census data, school records and government datasets. Most of it is in nobody’s records at all.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The centre reaches the young people who walk in. It does not know how many it is missing, or where they are. Outreach is guesswork.

The same blindness applies to what is around the centre. A tailoring unit two streets away that would take an apprentice, or a college with a free evening class, is invisible unless a staff member happens to know about it.
detail.whyNotFixed: Indian secondary data on young people is patchy, out of date, and published at the wrong level. District figures do not tell you about one neighbourhood. School dropout data exists but is held by different departments in different formats. Mapping community assets by hand takes weeks per neighbourhood and goes stale.
detail.whatExists: Ask Dream a Dream what mapping they have already tried, and what data they hold on the young people currently attending. Do not assume the answer is nothing. Finding out is the first piece of work.
detail.whatYouHave:
- published secondary data: census, education department records, state dashboards, open map data
- the location of at least one Thriving Centre as your test site
- possible fieldwork in that neighbourhood, subject to Dream a Dream’s consent process
detail.doneIn90Days: A map of one real neighbourhood around one real centre, plus the method you used to make it. The map has to answer two questions a centre manager will actually ask: which young people near us are we not reaching, and what is already here that we could use. The method matters as much as the map, because Dream a Dream needs to repeat this for the next centre without you.
detail.rules:
- every figure on the map carries its source and the year it refers to
- where data does not exist, the map says so rather than estimating
- no identifiable information about any young person appears in anything you hand over
- no household is surveyed door to door unless Dream a Dream is running the consent process
detail.findingYourApproach:
Around nine other teams are reading this same brief. Assume your first instinct is also theirs, and go looking for what makes the problem hard rather than what makes a demonstration look good.

Two questions worth arriving with: how do you estimate a population you cannot see, from public data that was never collected for this purpose, and what would make a centre manager still be updating your map a year after you have gone?
detail.sponsor:
Dream a Dream.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT. Strong fit for anyone interested in data science or geospatial work.
- **Technical skills** — Public data sourcing, geospatial analysis and mapping, estimation from incomplete data, data visualisation, survey design.
- **Other skills** — Judging source quality, stating uncertainty honestly, documenting a method someone else can repeat.

problems.title: Alumni and Mentor Network
problems.summary: Young people leave the centre and contact is lost. Keep it, and match them to mentors.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Dream a Dream, as described in Brief 01. This problem covers three of their questions at once: staying connected to alumni, helping young people learn from each other, and connecting them to people who can open doors.
detail.situation:
Young people spend time at a Thriving Centre, build skills and confidence, and then leave. Some go into work, some into further study, some into neither. The centre loses touch with almost all of them.

Meanwhile the young people still at the centre need two things the centre cannot supply on its own: someone slightly ahead of them who has done the thing they are trying to do, and someone outside their world who can make an introduction.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The alumni are the answer to the mentoring problem and nobody can find them. Phone numbers change. There is no reason to stay in touch, so nobody does.

Dream a Dream is explicit that the connection has to be worth something to the alumni too. A network that only asks past participants for favours will empty out.
detail.whyNotFixed: Alumni networks fail everywhere, including at wealthy universities with full-time staff running them. They fail for one reason: people join, nothing happens, they stop opening the emails. Building the database is a week of work. Making anyone come back is the actual problem, and it is a design problem more than a technical one.
detail.whatExists: An alumni contact list exists. It is unstructured and scattered, so expect to spend real time making it usable before you can do anything with it.
detail.whatYouHave:
- access to current Thriving Centre participants and facilitators for interviews, subject to consent
- access to alumni themselves, whose behaviour you most need to understand — reaching them is part of the work
- a pilot with a real group during your cycle is possible. Whether it happens is up to you to convince Dream a Dream
detail.doneIn90Days: Something real that a group of young people used, with evidence of whether they came back. A design document is not enough. Even a small pilot with twenty people over three weeks, with honest numbers about how many returned after the first session, is worth more than a polished app nobody opened.
detail.rules:
- contact details of young people stay under Dream a Dream’s control, not yours and not a third party’s
- no young person is matched with an outside adult without Dream a Dream’s safeguarding process in between
- the mechanism must give the alumni something, not only ask them for something
detail.findingYourApproach:
Alumni networks and mentor-matching schemes have been built many times, by organisations with far more money than Dream a Dream, and most of them are dead. Find out why before you design yours.

One question decides this project: why does anyone open it a second time? If you cannot answer that in a sentence, you do not have a proposal yet.
detail.sponsor:
Dream a Dream.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT. Suits students who want product and behaviour work rather than heavy engineering.
- **Technical skills** — Mobile-first and messaging-based interfaces, lightweight backend, matching logic, privacy-aware data handling.
- **Other skills** — Behavioural design, running a pilot and measuring it honestly, interviewing, safeguarding awareness.

problems.title: Youth Ownership of the Centre
problems.summary: Outside session hours the building is just a building. Make it usable by young people.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Dream a Dream, as described in Brief 01. This problem joins two of their questions: designing spaces that support the Thriving journey outside scheduled sessions, and designing spaces that invite young people to change them.
detail.situation: A Thriving Centre runs structured sessions at set times. Outside those hours the building is a building. Dream a Dream believes the important things — friendship, experimenting, belonging — happen in the unstructured time, and that the young people should be shaping the place, not visiting it.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
A room designed by adults for a programme signals who it belongs to. Fixed furniture, locked cupboards and finished walls all say: this is ours, you are a guest. Young people behave accordingly.

Dream a Dream’s words for the shift they want are moving young people “from participants to co-creators”. Right now the physical space works against that.
detail.whyNotFixed: Handing over a space sounds easy and is not. Someone still has to be responsible when something breaks, when two groups want the same room, or when a decision goes badly. Most attempts collapse into either adults quietly taking control back, or a free-for-all that staff then have to clean up. The design has to survive both.
detail.whatExists: Floor plans, photographs, an inventory of what is in the building and the terms it is held on may all exist somewhere. Finding out what exists, and getting hold of it, is your job.
detail.whatYouHave:
- site visits to at least one Thriving Centre, which you arrange yourselves
- the young people who use it, as co-designers rather than research subjects
- no materials budget at present. Anything you propose has to be cheap enough that the answer could change
detail.doneIn90Days: Something built and installed in a real centre, plus the rules that go with it. Both halves are required. A modular wall that young people can rearrange is useless without an answer to who decides, who fixes it, and what happens when it gets broken. Bring evidence that young people actually changed something after you left.
detail.rules:
- safe for children and young people, including when misused
- repairable by centre staff with ordinary tools and locally bought parts
- reversible — nothing that permanently damages a rented building
- designed with young people, not for them, with evidence of how they shaped it
detail.findingYourApproach:
Furniture is the easy half. The harder half is that a room designed by adults signals who it belongs to, and no amount of soft seating changes that.

The stronger position deals with governance as well as objects: what are young people actually allowed to decide, how is that decision made and recorded, and what stops staff quietly overruling it?
detail.sponsor:
Dream a Dream.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical, and any branch with an interest in design. One of the few problems in this pool with a physical build at its centre.
- **Technical skills** — Fabrication with basic tools, modular and flat-pack design, material selection and costing, safety assessment, prototyping.
- **Other skills** — Participatory design, facilitation, writing rules people will actually follow.

problems.title: Physical Education for Grades 1 to 10
problems.summary: One teacher, a wide range of ages and abilities, very little equipment.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Dream a Dream, as described in Brief 01. This problem sits inside their Thriving Schools programme, which works in government schools alongside the state curriculum.
detail.situation: Physical education is on the timetable from Grade 1 to Grade 10. One teacher takes a class that spans a wide range of ages, sizes, confidence levels and physical abilities. Equipment is limited. The state curriculum sets what must be covered.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Most PE sessions are one game, played by the children who are already good at it. The rest stand at the edge. A child who is smaller, slower, less confident, or disabled gets less activity, not more, which is the reverse of what PE is for.

Dream a Dream wants sessions that are inclusive, engaging and right for the age group, across a ten-grade range.
detail.whyNotFixed: The teacher is the bottleneck and cannot be replaced. Anything that requires a PE specialist, a lot of setup, or careful supervision of small groups will not survive contact with a real school day. Equipment that needs storing, charging or repairing disappears within a term.
detail.whatExists:
The state curriculum for physical education, which your work must align to rather than replace.

Which state, which curriculum document, what equipment the schools already have, and what Dream a Dream runs there now. Find all of that out early, because it shapes everything you design.
detail.whatYouHave:
- access to a school, a class and a PE teacher for testing. You will have to hustle for it
- class size, ground size and the current equipment list. Ask Dream a Dream when you meet them — these are good scoping questions
detail.doneIn90Days:
Something tested with real children in a real school, with evidence about who participated. The strongest measure is simple: count how many children in the class were physically active for how long, before and after. That single number is worth more than any amount of description.

Your output can be equipment, a set of activities, a way of grouping children, or a combination. It must work for a teacher with no specialist training.
detail.rules:
- safe for children, including unsupervised misuse
- aligned to the state curriculum, not a replacement for it
- cheap enough to put in many schools, and repairable locally
- inclusive by design, including for children with disabilities — not a separate activity for them
detail.findingYourApproach:
Be clear about what you are actually solving. The problem is not a shortage of equipment. It is that six children dominate any game with a ball in it while thirty stand at the edge.

Whatever you propose will be judged against one measure: how many children were physically active, and for how long. Work backwards from that number.
detail.sponsor:
Dream a Dream, Thriving Schools programme.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical, and any branch interested in design or sport. Little software content.
- **Technical skills** — Low-cost product design, fabrication, materials and durability, safety testing, designing for measurement.
- **Other skills** — Working with teachers and children, observation and measurement, inclusive design, curriculum reading.

problems.title: Finding a Child's Real Learning Level
problems.summary: A child enrolled in Grade 6 may read at Grade 2. Find the real level, at scale.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project SparkL is a Bengaluru trust, registered in 2022, that teaches foundational reading and arithmetic to children from vulnerable backgrounds, including children living in shelter homes. It runs after-school evening sessions at seven centres for about 130 to 140 children, with two partner organisations.
detail.situation:
The children SparkL works with are enrolled in a school grade that does not match what they can actually do. A child may be registered in Grade 6 and be unable to read a Grade 2 sentence.

SparkL already handles this properly. It assesses each child in Kannada, Maths and English across grade levels, works out a “skill grade”, and builds a learning plan from that rather than from the school grade. This is the core of their method and it works.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The method is manual, so it stops at seven centres. Assessing each child, working out the skill grade, planning the teaching and tracking progress all depend on a small number of people doing it by hand.

SparkL wants to reach more children. Right now growth means hiring proportionally, which is the definition of a model that will not scale.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Off-the-shelf learning apps assume the child’s grade is their level, which is precisely the assumption that fails here. Adaptive learning products assume a smartphone per child, reliable internet and a literate parent nearby. None of those hold in a shelter home in the evening.

There is also a harder problem. Assessing a child in three languages, including Kannada, without a trained adult listening to them read, is genuinely difficult.
detail.whatExists:
SparkL’s own assessment approach and skill-grade system. Do not replace it — understand it first, then work out which parts a machine can carry. Facilitator training is a separate problem and is covered by Brief 19; coordinate with whoever takes it, because you are both working on how SparkL grows past seven centres.

The assessment materials, how the skill grade is worked out, and what records SparkL keeps today may all be available. Ask for them.
detail.whatYouHave:
- sample assessment records, anonymised progress data and session plans, if you can persuade SparkL to share them
- a session at a centre to sit in on, if you arrange it. Watching one is worth more than any document
- the educators who run the sessions, who know more about this than any document will tell you
detail.doneIn90Days:
One part of the loop, working, tested with real records. That could be the assessment itself, the skill-grade calculation, the learning plan, or the progress tracking. Choose one and make it good enough that SparkL would use it next term.

It must work in Kannada as well as English, on a shared low-end device, and without assuming internet during the session.
detail.rules:
- no identifiable data about any child leaves SparkL’s control, and none goes into a third-party service without written agreement — several of these children are in shelter homes
- Kannada is not an afterthought or a translated label — the assessment has to work in it
- works offline during a session, syncs later
- an educator with no technical training can run it
detail.findingYourApproach:
Understand SparkL’s existing method properly before you automate any part of it. The educators have already solved problems you have not thought of.

Then two questions decide whether SparkL could use what you build. How do you assess a child’s reading without an adult listening to them? And what happens on the evening the internet is down and the tablet is at 8%?
detail.sponsor:
Project SparkL.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT.
- **Technical skills** — Offline-first application design, speech or audio processing for reading assessment, adaptive logic, multilingual and Indic-script interfaces, data privacy.
- **Other skills** — Working with educators, assessment design, writing for children, understanding a method before automating it.

problems.title: Two-Wheeler Technician Training
problems.summary: A 60 hour hands-on programme across petrol and electric two-wheelers, and the workshop to run it.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project SparkL, described in Brief 06. This problem comes from Project Scale Up, their work on making the organisation financially sustainable rather than grant-dependent.
detail.situation:
SparkL wants to run a 60-hour hands-on training programme for young people aged 18 to 25 from ITI and Polytechnic backgrounds. It covers petrol vehicles, electric vehicles, scooters and motorcycles, and needs workshop infrastructure and practical exposure to work at all.

SparkL has also identified a second gap: young people finish formal qualifications without the workplace skills that get them hired — communication, spreadsheets, presentations, email.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: An ITI or Polytechnic certificate does not make someone employable in a two-wheeler workshop. The training is theory-heavy and the equipment is often a generation behind the vehicles on the road. Electric two-wheelers are the sharpest version of this: battery packs, controllers, motor diagnostics and high-voltage safety are absent from most curricula.
detail.whyNotFixed: Hands-on training is expensive. It needs vehicles, tools, space and a trainer per small group. Manufacturer training programmes exist but are closed to their own dealer networks. Sixty hours is a real constraint: it is enough to make someone useful at a narrow set of tasks and nowhere near enough to make a general technician.
detail.whatExists:
Atria University and Atria Institute of Technology have an e-mobility department, which currently holds the Atria Foundation food truck for an electric powertrain conversion. That department is the most obvious source of equipment, expertise and workshop space for this problem.

Whether SparkL has drafted any of the curriculum, and whether workshop space or vehicles have been secured, is for you to find out.
detail.whatYouHave:
- workshop space, tools and vehicles to train on. Securing these is part of the project
- trainee candidates to test the material on, whom you will have to recruit
- the Atria e-mobility department, which holds the equipment and the expertise. Whether they take part is up to you to arrange
detail.doneIn90Days:
A section of the 60 hours, built and taught to real people at least once, with evidence of what they could do afterwards that they could not do before. That means the trainer notes, the equipment list with costs, the practical exercises, and the assessment that proves competence.

An employer’s view is what matters. “Completed the module” is worth nothing. “Can diagnose a controller fault in under fifteen minutes” is worth something.
detail.rules:
- high-voltage safety is taught and enforced before anyone touches a battery pack — this is not negotiable
- the equipment list has to be affordable for a small training centre, with current prices and dates
- the material must be teachable by a trainer who is a good mechanic, not an engineer
- assessment proves a task can be done, not that a class was attended
detail.findingYourApproach:
Sixty hours is the constraint that shapes everything. The useful question is not what a technician should know, but what you can honestly teach in sixty hours that gets someone hired.

Talk to a workshop owner before you write a single line of syllabus. Ask what they actually test when somebody walks in looking for work.
detail.sponsor:
Project SparkL, Project Scale Up.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical and Electronics. The strongest Mech and EC problem in this pool.
- **Technical skills** — Electric and internal combustion powertrains, battery systems, motor controllers, diagnostics, workshop practice, electrical safety, tooling and costing.
- **Other skills** — Teaching and instructional design, competence assessment, talking to employers about what they hire for.

problems.title: Communications Analytics Dashboard
problems.summary: Website, social, email and payment data sit in eight places and never form one picture.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
The Centre for Wildlife Studies is a Bengaluru research and conservation organisation, working for around four decades on wildlife research, conservation, policy and education. Its programmes include Wild Seve, Wild Shaale, Wild Surakshe and a doctoral programme. Wild Seve alone has filed over 35,000 compensation claims for more than 17,000 families in over 4,000 settlements since 2015.

This problem comes from the Media and Outreach team, and CWS ranked it their first priority.
detail.situation: CWS communicates and fundraises through a website, Google Analytics, Google Search Console, Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube, Flodesk for email, Razorpay for payments, and campaign activity on top. Each holds a piece of the picture. None of them talk to each other.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Somebody logs into eight systems every month, copies numbers into a spreadsheet, and builds a report. It takes hours, it happens late, and it produces figures nobody can act on quickly enough to change a campaign that is failing.
detail.whyNotFixed: The platforms make it hard on purpose. Instagram and LinkedIn restrict their data access, YouTube and GA4 have their own models and quotas, and Flodesk and Razorpay are small enough that their access options are limited. Some of these have no usable interface for automated access at all, which means part of this job is not integration but designing an honest manual step that does not rot.
detail.whatExists:
The current monthly reporting process, whatever it is. Understand it before replacing it — the person who builds that spreadsheet knows which numbers matter and which are noise.

Ask how the monthly report is built today, which platform accounts you could be given, and whether anyone has tried to automate it before.
detail.whatYouHave:
- read-only access to each platform, which CWS has to grant. This is the single biggest thing to settle in week one
- historical exports to build and test against, if CWS will share them
- the Media and Outreach team, who will tell you what they actually look at
detail.doneIn90Days: A dashboard the CWS team opens instead of building the spreadsheet. It refreshes on its own where the platform allows it, and has a clear, documented manual step where it does not. Every metric has a written definition, so two people reading it agree on what it means. It comes with a handover document, because you leave and CWS keeps it.
detail.rules:
- no donor personal data from Razorpay or Flodesk goes anywhere it should not, including into a chart
- credentials are never stored in the code or the repository
- a person who is not a programmer must be able to keep it running after you leave
- where a number is manually entered, the dashboard says so
detail.findingYourApproach:
Several teams will land on the same tool over exported spreadsheets, and it is not obviously the wrong answer. That means visuals will not separate you.

Maintenance will. Who refreshes the export, what happens when a platform renames a column, and why is your answer better than the spreadsheet it replaces? Treat this as a data engineering and handover problem rather than a charting problem.
detail.sponsor:
CWS Media and Outreach team. Note that this team also sponsors Brief 09, so their time is split.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT.
- **Technical skills** — Working with third-party interfaces and their limits, scheduled jobs, data modelling, dashboard and chart design, credential handling.
- **Other skills** — Defining metrics unambiguously, writing documentation someone else can follow, designing for handover.

problems.title: Find Anything CWS Has
problems.summary: Two large archives of photos, video and approved facts, with no way to find anything.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: CWS Media and Outreach, as described in Brief 08. This brief combines two of their requests, ranked second and third, because both are the same problem: finding what CWS already has.
detail.situation:
Two archives. One is a large and growing set of photographs and videos in Google Drive folders. The other is a set of documents holding approved statistics, programme information and institutional facts — the numbers CWS is allowed to publish.

A staff member writing a grant application or a press response needs both, quickly, and needs to know the number is current and approved.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Finding a photograph means remembering which folder it is in and who took it. Finding a statistic means asking a colleague, who may give you last year’s figure. A wrong number in a grant application or a news article is a real cost to a research organisation.
detail.whyNotFixed: Drive search reads filenames, and a filename like IMG_4471.jpg tells you nothing. Adding metadata to thousands of existing files by hand is more work than anyone has time for. For the documents, the problem is different: the difficulty is not searching but knowing which version is the approved one and who approved it.
detail.whatExists:
Google Drive, which stays as the storage. CWS is explicit that they do not want to move their files. Whatever you build sits on top and links back to the original.

Find out how large the archive is, how the folders are organised, what naming conventions already exist, and which documents count as approved.
detail.whatYouHave:
- access to a defined set of Drive folders for the prototype, agreed with CWS
- a controlled set of approved documents. CWS has indicated dummy or current data can be used
- CWS has mentioned possible Slack integration as a nice-to-have, not a requirement
detail.doneIn90Days:
Someone at CWS types a plain question and gets a useful answer. For an image: find photographs by programme, species, location, date, photographer, event, asset type and usage rights, with a link to the file in Drive. For a fact: give the answer, its source document, its date and a link — never the answer alone.

It also needs a repeatable way to add new material, or it stops being true within a month.
detail.rules:
- every answer carries its source, its date and a link — an answer without a source is a defect, not a feature
- the system must say “I do not know” rather than produce a plausible number
- Drive permissions are respected — the search must not show someone a file they cannot open
- usage rights on photographs are surfaced, because publishing an image CWS does not have rights to is a legal problem
detail.findingYourApproach:
The interesting question is not how to make it answer. It is what happens when it answers confidently and wrongly.

A wildlife organisation quoting a fabricated conflict statistic in a press release is worse off than with no tool at all. Work out how your system knows that it does not know, and design the human check that catches whatever gets through.
detail.sponsor:
CWS Media and Outreach team, who also sponsor Brief 08.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT.
- **Technical skills** — Search and retrieval, document and image indexing, vision models for tagging, metadata design, permissions, evaluating a system for factual accuracy.
- **Other skills** — Information architecture, designing a process people will keep using, testing for failure rather than for success.

problems.title: Donor Relationship Prototype
problems.summary: Donor touchpoints are scattered and never become one relationship history.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: The CWS Fundraising team. This is a different team from Briefs 08 and 09, with its own priorities and its own contact.
detail.situation:
People come into contact with CWS through email, digital campaigns, events and donations. Each of those leaves a record somewhere. Together they never form one history of a relationship.

CWS deals with two very different groups. Foundations, trusts and companies give large amounts on a reporting cycle with formal requirements. Individuals give small amounts, irregularly, and respond to completely different things.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Nobody can answer basic questions. How did this donor first hear about us? What have we sent them? What are they interested in? When should we contact them next? Without that, fundraising is a series of disconnected asks, and the people most likely to give again are treated like strangers.
detail.whyNotFixed: Commercial fundraising software exists and is priced for organisations much larger than CWS. Salesforce and similar tools are free or discounted for non-profits and then need a paid consultant to configure and maintain. The real question is not what to build but whether to build at all — and CWS has explicitly asked for that recommendation.
detail.whatExists:
Records sit in Flodesk, Razorpay, event lists and spreadsheets. CWS has also specifically asked to explore connecting this system to an AI assistant, so that lead history, next-step reminders and call notes stay in one place with less manual updating.

What records exist, in what systems and in what state, is your first question for the Fundraising team.
detail.whatYouHave:
- dummy or sample data — CWS has said this is acceptable and expected
- the Fundraising team, who can describe how a donor relationship actually develops
- real anonymised data, if CWS agrees to share any. Plan on dummy data and treat anything real as a bonus
detail.doneIn90Days:
Two things, and the second matters more than the first.

- a working prototype on sample data showing acquisition source, interests, campaign engagement, communication history, contributions, separate handling of organisational and individual donors, and a suggested next step
- a written recommendation on whether CWS should build, buy or adapt, with real costs and a clear reason — including the honest answer, if it is the right one, that CWS should not build this
detail.rules:
- use dummy data by default; treat any real record as confidential
- organisational and individual donors are modelled differently, because they behave differently
- an automated next-step suggestion is a suggestion to a human, never an automatic email to a donor
- the recommendation is evidence-based, with real prices, not an opinion
detail.findingYourApproach:
A contact database with a dashboard demonstrates well and answers a question CWS did not ask.

They asked whether they should build at all. Take that seriously enough to be willing to argue against building. And take their request to connect this to an AI assistant seriously enough to work out what it would actually mean for call notes and follow-ups.

CWS Fundraising team.

problems.title: Identifying Species by Sound
problems.summary: Field recorders produce enormous audio. Most of it is wind. Find the calls that matter.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: The CWS Research team. This is the third CWS team in this pool and the one with the highest standards for what it accepts.
detail.situation:
CWS places acoustic recorders in the field to monitor species. The recorders produce enormous quantities of audio, most of it wind, rain, insects and silence. Somewhere in it are the calls that matter.

An engineering student is already building a classifier that identifies species from these recordings. It works. There is more data and more analysis than one person can get through.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: The bottleneck is labelled data and validation, not model architecture. Someone has to listen to clips and confirm what is in them, and until that exists the classifier cannot be extended to new species or trusted for new sites.
detail.whyNotFixed: Labelling audio is slow and needs someone who can tell two similar calls apart. Field recordings are noisy in ways that clean training data is not. And a classifier used in research has to be right in a way a demo does not: a false positive in a species survey is a false scientific claim.
detail.whatExists:
The existing classifier and the student building it. Coordinate with them from week one. Rebuilding what already works, in parallel, is the main way this project wastes a cycle.

The classifier’s architecture, which species it covers, how accurate it is, and how much labelled audio exists. Establish all four in your first conversation with the Research team.
detail.whatYouHave:
- CWS acoustic recordingsCWS acoustic recordings. Volume, format and how they reach you are for you to agree with the Research team
- the Research team, who will set the exact scope with you
- the engineering student already on the project

CWS has said the scope here is likely to change as more labelled audio and classifier results come in. Treat this brief as a starting point, not a specification.
detail.doneIn90Days:
One bounded, agreed piece of work, finished to a standard CWS can cite. That is likely to be one of: a trained model for one additional species, a validated labelled dataset, or an accuracy evaluation of the existing classifier.

Research intends to use this in its own scientific output. Your methods, data handling and results must be documented to peer-reviewed standards. A working demo with no reproducible method is a failed project here, even if the model performs well.
detail.rules:
- peer-reviewed documentation standard: reproducible method, stated assumptions, honest error rates
- report what the model gets wrong, not only what it gets right
- data stays confidential and is not uploaded to a public service without permission — recordings can reveal the location of threatened species
- scope agreed with the Research team and the existing student before you start building
- nothing about CWS data is published without their agreement
detail.findingYourApproach:
The standard approach to this is well documented and every team will find it. Finding it is not the contribution.

What it hides is the interesting part. The target species may appear in a tiny fraction of clips, accuracy may be the wrong measure entirely, and a field ecologist has to be able to check your result. Design for those three and you will have something CWS can publish.

CWS Research team. Note that CWS ranked this fifth of seven, so expect less of their attention than Briefs 08 to 10.

- **Branch** — Electronics and CS. One of the few problems here with genuine signal processing content.
- **Technical skills** — Audio signal processing, machine learning for classification, dataset construction and labelling, evaluation under class imbalance, reproducible research practice.
- **Other skills** — Scientific writing, working inside someone else’s project, reporting negative results honestly.

problems.title: The LoveAll Transparency Ledger
problems.summary: Put charitable fund flow on a ledger so a donor can see exactly where the money went.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Atria Foundation is the charitable arm of Atria Group. It runs food kitchens and food trucks, the Atria Mega Skill Centre, healthcare initiatives and plantation drives. Its stated numbers include over 1.7 crore cumulative meals served, more than 4,000 people trained in trades such as tailoring, hospitality and IT, and around 620 placed with employers including KPR Mills, Arvind Mills, Hotel Leela Palace and Reliance Trends. It operates around 20 kitchens across roughly 255 locations with 200 or more volunteers.

LoveAll is its social loyalty card. Members pay ₹1,000 a year, get discounts across a network of Bengaluru restaurants and retailers, and their money funds four causes: Food, Education, Healthcare and Bio-Diversity.
detail.situation:
LoveAll makes a promise most charities do not: that you can see exactly where your money went. The Foundation states it is moving its fund flow onto a blockchain so that transparency is coded in rather than promised.

The programme also wants to grow beyond funding Atria Foundation’s own work, and become a funding engine that other registered NGOs can plug into. That ambition is where the difficulty lives.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Nothing is broken yet. The promise has been made and the system that would keep it does not exist. Right now a member who asks “what did my ₹1,000 do” gets an aggregate number, not a traceable answer.

The harder problem is that a naive ledger would be wrong in a way that matters. Indian tax law treats “we spent money on our own programme” and “we gave money to another NGO” completely differently. A ledger that reports ₹1,00,000 sent to a partner NGO as ₹1,00,000 of impact misstates the Foundation’s tax position, even when the partner genuinely spent every rupee.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Four sets of rules apply at the same time, and satisfying one while ignoring another still leaves you non-compliant:

- **Income Tax Act** — a registered charity must apply at least 85% of its income to charitable purposes each year. Since the Finance Act 2023, a general donation from one registered NGO to another counts as only 85% application for the giver. Corpus donations do not count at all
- **Companies Act, Section 135** — for corporate money to count as CSR, the receiving entity must be registered on Form CSR-1 and hold valid 12AB and 80G
- **FCRA** — since the 2020 amendment, passing foreign contributions on to any other organisation is prohibited outright. This is a hard stop, not a tax inefficiency
- **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023** — requires that personal data can be corrected and erased. A blockchain cannot easily erase anything. The main obligations are expected around May 2027

That last one is the genuine engineering tension in this problem, and nobody in the industry has solved it cleanly.
detail.whatExists:
An 18-page context brief prepared by the Foundation, covering the fund-flow map, the stakeholder map, the four pillars, the original blockchain rationale and the full compliance picture. It deliberately stops short of proposing an architecture. Read it before you pitch — this is by far the best-prepared problem in this pool.

Registrations already in place: 12AB, 80G and CSR-1. Ground-truth data already being collected includes a mandatory daily photo submission from the food trucks and field check-ins, which the brief suggests could feed attestations.

The Foundation’s technology stack document exists as a Google Doc and could not be extracted into the context brief. It likely already defines the app and database layer your work would sit alongside, so ask for it early.
detail.whatYouHave:
- the 18-page LoveAll context brief, including four diagrams: the fund-flow map, the four-pillar structure, a conceptual attestation pipeline, and the compliance layers
- Atria Institute of Technology and Atria University, named in the brief as a possible source of technical and build support
- the technology stack document, sample transaction data and the current app or database, all of which you will have to ask for
detail.doneIn90Days:
A working prototype of one part of the pipeline, on simulated payments, that a compliance-minded reader would accept. The context brief names five building blocks worth prototyping:

- a member ledger that recognises donors without putting their personal data on a chain
- a fund pool where every inflow is tagged Food, Education, Healthcare, Bio-Diversity or Operations at the point of entry
- a disbursement contract that releases funds only when a real-world event is attested — a delivery photo, a placement record, a plantation record
- a routing module for transfers to partner NGOs that carries the compliance metadata with it
- a public dashboard showing aggregated figures without exposing personal data

Pick one or two. Make the compliance behaviour real, not commented out.
detail.rules:
- no raw personal data on any chain, public or permissioned — hashes, pseudonymous identifiers or aggregates only, with the real records held off-chain where they can be corrected or deleted
- every inflow is tagged at entry on three axes: domestic or foreign, corpus or general, and CSR or donation or membership fee
- foreign-tagged funds can never be routed to a partner NGO. The system must make this impossible, not merely discouraged
- a transfer to a partner NGO carries an automatic 15% ineligible-application tag — do not model it as a 100% pass-through of value
- the ledger must not split a ₹1,000 payment into a donation part and a membership-fee part
- the same rupee is never presented as both CSR-eligible and 80G-deductible
- you design to the legal constraints; you do not give legal or tax advice, and qualified professionals confirm them
- no token that could be traded or held as value is ever issued
detail.findingYourApproach:
Ten teams left alone with the word blockchain will build ten token ledgers. Do not be one of them until you have argued the question properly.

Four questions decide a serious proposal. Does a chain earn its place here, against a signed append-only log with published hashes and an independent auditor? Who or what attests that a thousand meals were served, and why should anyone believe that source? Who holds the signing keys for a charity, and what happens when they are lost? And at ₹1,000 a membership, do per-transaction costs make your design uneconomic?

One thing to raise with the sponsor. The context brief treats 80G as making the ₹1,000 tax-attractive and mentions a “50% tax rebate” in the corporate pitch. Under India’s new personal tax regime, now the default, Chapter VI-A deductions including 80G are generally not available to individuals. Confirm this before you build any part of the story around it.
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation, LoveAll Card. Contact given in the brief: contact@atriafoundation.org, +91 8971101055.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT. The most demanding software problem in this pool.
- **Technical skills** — Distributed ledgers and smart contracts, cryptographic hashing and signatures, key management, systems design under regulatory constraint, privacy-preserving data design, payment flows.
- **Other skills** — Reading legislation and turning rules into system behaviour, arguing an architecture decision on evidence, explaining a technical design to a non-technical trustee.

problems.title: Proving a Tree Is Still Alive
problems.summary: A sponsor pays for a tree and needs auditable proof that it is alive years later.
skills: Mobile data capture and offline sync

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Project Chitoor is a rural development project working across roughly 20 clusters with around 50 ground workers and about 250 families. It has three parts: farming and processing, education, and environment.

Its legal entity, exact location and funding structure are not set out here. Establish them before you design anything that touches money.
detail.situation: The project wants to open a funding channel where a company or an individual pays to plant a tree and, in a meaningful sense, owns it. Companies with CSR obligations need reporting they can put in front of an auditor. Individuals need something that feels real.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Tree donation schemes have a credibility problem, and it is deserved. Many amount to a certificate and a stock photograph. A donor has no way to check that a specific tree was planted, is still alive, or was not sold to three other donors.

The project cannot fix this by sending updates by hand. With 50 ground workers already stretched, a scheme that needs a staff member to photograph each tree each quarter will die in its first year.
detail.whyNotFixed: Verifying that a specific tree in a field is alive is genuinely hard and genuinely boring. Satellite imagery cannot resolve one sapling. GPS drifts by metres. Tags fall off, fade, and get eaten. And whatever you design has to be done by a farm worker with a phone in one hand, at scale, for years, without anyone reminding them.
detail.whatExists:
Trees are already being planted as part of the project’s environment work.

How many trees have been planted, whether any are recorded or located, and whether a donation channel exists today. All open, all findable.
detail.whatYouHave:
- a real plantation site to pilot tracking on actual trees, which you will have to arrange
- the ground staff who would operate whatever you design. Talk to them early, or you will design something they will not use
- payments can be simulated; you do not need a live payment gateway
detail.doneIn90Days:
Four things, working end to end on a small number of real trees:

- a payment triggers assignment of a specific tree, creating a record with donor, amount, tree identifier, location and planting date
- a way to check on that tree over time that ground staff will actually keep doing
- reports generated and sent on a schedule, with nobody compiling them
- an audit trail linking money to tree to outcome that would survive a CSR auditor’s questions

Pilot it on ten real trees rather than simulating a thousand.
detail.rules:
- do not promise donors tax deductibility. The project has stated that the 80G deduction is not available under India’s new tax regime, so the reporting has to sell transparency and impact instead
- tracking must be something a ground worker can do in seconds, in a field, on a basic phone, possibly offline
- the link from money to tree to outcome must be auditable end to end
- if a tree dies, the system must be able to say so. A scheme that cannot report a failure is not a transparency system
detail.findingYourApproach:
Whatever mechanism you choose, one question will find the hole in it. What stops a busy worker recording fifty trees from the shade without looking at any of them?

A design that cannot answer that is a reporting system, not a verification system, and the donors it is built for will eventually work that out.
detail.sponsor:
Project Chitoor. Note this team also sponsors Briefs 14 to 17.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT, with room for Electronics students on the sensing side.
- **Technical skills** — Payment and workflow automation, mobile data capture, offline sync, geolocation, image verification, scheduled reporting, audit trail design.
- **Other skills** — Designing for people who will not be trained, thinking about how a system gets gamed, understanding what an auditor needs.

problems.title: Solar Dryer Trays That Turn Themselves
problems.summary: Loading, turning, checking and unloading solar dryer trays is all manual and repeats daily.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project Chitoor, described in Brief 13. Around 50 ground workers across 20 clusters do sorting, harvesting support, solar dryer handling, irrigation valve management, sheep feed distribution, deweeding and planting — all by hand.
detail.situation: Solar dryers reduce harvested produce to a storable, sellable form. Trays are loaded, turned during drying so material dries evenly, checked repeatedly for dryness, and unloaded when done. All of it is manual and all of it repeats every day the sun is out.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Two separate problems in one place. The physical handling costs hours of labour per day and does not get cheaper as the project grows. And judging dryness by hand and eye is unreliable: under-dried produce spoils, over-dried produce loses weight and value.
detail.whyNotFixed: Commercial drying equipment with automated handling and moisture control exists and is priced for industrial processors. It needs stable mains power, spare parts from a city supplier, and a technician when it breaks. On a working farm with unreliable grid power and no technician within reach, that equipment becomes an expensive shed ornament within a season.
detail.whatExists:
Solar dryers are already installed and in daily use. You are improving them, not replacing them.

Dryer type and dimensions, tray size and weight, what produce is dried, target moisture levels, and current daily labour hours. Go and measure them.
detail.whatYouHave:
- site access at Chitoor to measure the dryers and test on them. Arranging it is your first job
- a workshop, tools and a materials budget, none of which is guaranteed. Design for cheap
- ground staff who do this work daily and know where it is worst

Site access is the make-or-break dependency on this brief. Settle it in week one.
detail.doneIn90Days:
A working prototype installed and running at one block, plus two numbers: labour hours for that task before and after, measured rather than estimated, and a cost breakdown for rolling it out across more blocks.

You may take the handling, the moisture sensing, or both. Both is ambitious.
detail.rules:
- low cost, and repairable locally — no proprietary parts that need a technician from the city
- runs on solar or battery power, because the grid is not reliable on site
- rugged enough for daily use on a working farm, not a laboratory demonstration
- fits the existing infrastructure rather than requiring a rebuild
- safe for workers who have had no training on it
detail.findingYourApproach:
Before you design anything, watch the task being done and time it. The parts that look hardest are rarely where the hours go.

Then design for failure rather than for the demonstration: what happens when a bearing seizes with dust in it, whether a worker can clear a jam without tools, and whether your moisture reading tracks the produce being dry or only the surface being dry.
detail.sponsor:
Project Chitoor.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical, with Electronics on the sensing and control side.
- **Technical skills** — Mechanism design, fabrication and welding, materials for outdoor use, solar and battery power, sensors and microcontrollers, calibration, cost engineering.
- **Other skills** — Measuring a process before changing it, designing for repair, working alongside people who will use what you build.

problems.title: Taking Weeds Out Without Taking the Crop
problems.summary: Weeding is hand work all season, and the labour grows with every acre farmed.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project Chitoor, described in Brief 13.
detail.situation: Weeds are removed by hand across the project’s blocks. It is repetitive, it is physically hard, it happens continuously through the growing season, and the labour needed grows in direct proportion to the area farmed.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: This task alone consumes a large share of the 50 ground workers’ time. Every hour spent deweeding is an hour not spent on work that expands the project. It is the clearest example of a task that blocks growth.
detail.whyNotFixed: Weeding machinery exists for large monoculture farms with wide, regular rows and tractors to pull it. Project Chitoor has blocks and clusters, not prairie. Herbicides are the other standard answer and are unattractive for a project built around sustainability. And the core difficulty is real: a machine has to remove a plant growing next to another plant without damaging the roots of the one you want.
detail.whatExists:
Crops grown, row spacing, block layout, soil type and current tools — and how many labour hours deweeding takes now. That last figure matters more than any other on this brief, and only you can go and get it.

That last figure matters more than any other on this brief. Without it you cannot prove your machine helped.
detail.whatYouHave:
- site access to measure real rows and test in real soil
- a workshop, tools and a materials budget, none of which is guaranteed
detail.doneIn90Days: A working machine, tested in a real block, with before-and-after labour hours for that block and a cost breakdown for building more. Crop damage must be measured, not assumed to be zero.
detail.rules:
- crop roots are not damaged, and you have to show this with measurements
- low cost and locally repairable, with no proprietary parts
- solar or battery compatible if it is powered at all
- rugged for daily use, and operable by a worker with no training
detail.findingYourApproach:
Measure the baseline before you build. Without knowing how many labour hours deweeding takes today, you cannot show your machine helped, and neither can Project Chitoor.

Then take on the unglamorous questions, because they are what decides it: uneven ground, what happens when the mechanism hits a stone, and whether one person can push it for four hours without their back giving out.
detail.sponsor:
Project Chitoor.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical. The purest mechanical engineering problem in this pool.
- **Technical skills** — Mechanism and linkage design, soil and tool interaction, fabrication, ergonomics, materials and wear, cost engineering, field testing.
- **Other skills** — Measuring a baseline before you change anything, iterating from failure, designing for the person who has to use it all day.

problems.title: Planting Faster and Straighter
problems.summary: Saplings, slips and seeds are placed by hand, with depth and spacing varying all day.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project Chitoor, described in Brief 13.
detail.situation: Three kinds of planting happen across the project: saplings, slips or rows, and seeds. All are placed by hand. Depth, spacing and placement vary with whoever is doing it and how tired they are.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Planting is slow, and inconsistent planting costs twice. It costs labour hours now, and it costs yield later, because a sapling planted too deep or too close to its neighbour grows badly. The project describes planting as one of its highest-frequency tasks, which makes it a strong candidate for an early win.
detail.whyNotFixed: Mechanical planters exist for single crops at industrial scale. This project plants three different things in different layouts, in blocks rather than long rows, sometimes on uneven ground. A machine built for one of those cases is useless for the others, and buying three is not affordable.
detail.whatExists: What is planted, the depth and spacing each needs, the current planting rate per worker, the terrain and the soil. Find all of it out before you draw anything.
detail.whatYouHave:
- site access, and a planting cycle to test during. Check the calendar early — if planting season falls outside your window you need a different test plan
- a workshop, tools and a materials budget, none of which is guaranteed

Timing matters more here than on other briefs. If planting season falls outside your cycle, agree an alternative test arrangement in week one.
detail.doneIn90Days: A jig or mechanism used by real workers during real planting, with measurements: planting rate before and after, and how consistent the depth and spacing became. A cost breakdown for making more.
detail.rules:
- low cost and locally repairable
- works on uneven ground and in real soil conditions
- light enough to be carried and used all day by one person
- faster than doing it by hand, proven with a measurement rather than a claim
detail.findingYourApproach:
Find out where the time actually goes before you design a thing. Marking positions, making holes, placing plants and covering them are four separate tasks, and only one of them is your bottleneck.

Cheap and old often wins here. Judge every idea against one test: is it faster than a hand, measured rather than claimed?
detail.sponsor:
Project Chitoor.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical.
- **Technical skills** — Jig and fixture design, mechanism design, ergonomics, fabrication, materials, time and motion measurement, cost engineering.
- **Other skills** — Observing work as it is actually done, iterating with the people who use the tool, resisting over-engineering.

problems.title: Why Nobody Uses the Tablets
problems.summary: Tablets and a learning platform are in the school. Adoption stalled. Find out why, then fix it.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Project Chitoor, described in Brief 13. This problem sits in its education work, which the project says is part of its story to investors and press.
detail.situation:
Tablets and a learning platform have been given to students at the local school. The money is spent and the equipment is there.

Adoption has stalled. The project names three reasons: teachers are unwilling to push usage because it is extra work on top of an existing load, the electricity supply is unreliable, and the internet is inconsistent.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Expensive hardware is going unused, so the educational benefit is not happening and the story told to donors is not true. Both of those matter to the project.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Because the usual fix is to ask teachers to try harder, and teachers already have a full day. Any solution resting on goodwill will work for three weeks and then stop. The project is explicit that it wants a system that does not depend on teacher goodwill alone.

There is also a real possibility nobody has tested: that the stated reasons are not the actual reasons. Nobody has done the diagnosis.
detail.whatExists:
The tablets and the platform, both already deployed. You must work within them — the project has ruled out proposing replacement hardware.

Which tablets, which platform, how many, how many teachers and students, and what usage data the platform already records. All of that is yours to establish.
detail.whatYouHave:
- access to the school, its teachers and its classrooms. This is the same cooperation that is already missing, so winning it is part of the problem
- whatever usage logs the platform already produces, if you can get hold of them

School access is the critical dependency, and it is the same cooperation that is already missing. If you cannot get into a classroom, you cannot do this project. Confirm it in week one.
detail.doneIn90Days:
Four things:

- a diagnosis of why adoption is low, backed by data rather than opinion, that says which factor matters most
- an intervention designed from that diagnosis and piloted with at least one teacher or classroom
- a before-and-after comparison of actual usage
- a recommendation on whether and how to roll it out to other schools

The diagnosis is the deliverable that has the most value. If you find that the real barrier is something nobody named, that finding alone justifies the project.
detail.rules:
- work with the hardware already deployed
- account for the real electricity and internet situation rather than assuming it improves
- any process change must add close to zero effort for teachers
- the result must be runnable by school staff or a small support team after you leave
- usage measurement must not depend on teachers reporting it themselves
detail.findingYourApproach:
Notice what your first instinct assumes. Most approaches to this problem assume infrastructure is the barrier, while Project Chitoor’s own description puts teacher workload first.

Find out which is true before you build anything. A team willing to report that the hardware was the wrong purchase will produce something more useful than a team that starts building in week two.
detail.sponsor:
Project Chitoor, education work.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.

- **Branch** — CS and IT for the software and monitoring, Electronics for power and connectivity. Also suits students who want research and fieldwork.
- **Technical skills** — Offline-first content delivery, local caching and syncing, low-power and battery-backed systems, usage logging and analysis, Android device management.
- **Other skills** — Structured root-cause investigation, interviewing people who may not tell you the real reason, designing a pilot, reporting an unwelcome finding.

problems.title: The Value Chain Research Engine
problems.summary: Map a value chain end to end before deciding where energy technology changes an income.
skills: Language models under a factual constraint

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
SELCO Foundation is a Bengaluru-registered trust working on sustainable energy access for underserved communities, using decentralised renewable energy to reduce poverty and improve livelihoods. It works across agriculture, animal husbandry, textiles and crafts, micro-businesses, healthcare and the built environment, with documented work in Karnataka, Odisha, Jharkhand and Assam.

This request comes from its Innovation Team, which designs the energy-enabled livelihood work and needs to understand a value chain before it can place a solution inside it.
detail.situation:
Before SELCO can decide where a solar dryer or a cold room actually changes someone’s income, it needs to know how a value chain works end to end — who does what, where value is created and lost, where energy and technology are missing, and where a farmer or artisan could move up into being an enterprise.

SELCO needs this for 32 value chains, of which 13 are the priority: rice and paddy, turmeric, millet, pineapple, mushroom, honey, IoT irrigation, poultry, piggery, cane and bamboo, silk, eateries and cafes, and snack making. Each one becomes a presentation following a fixed ten-section structure covering lifecycle, nodal points, stakeholders, challenges, package of practices, technology interventions, capacity building, enterprise opportunities, the SELCO opportunity and income impact.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The research itself is the bottleneck. Each chain means working through Government of India ministry reports, NABARD and SFAC publications, ICAR material, commodity board data from bodies such as the Spices Board and the Central Silk Board, and state department figures — then extracting comparable information into an identical structure.

SELCO’s quality bar is what makes this hard rather than merely long. Every figure, cost, yield, price and claim must carry a named source with a link or full citation. Unsourced numbers are rejected. Where data does not exist, the gap must be stated plainly rather than filled with a plausible estimate — a draft with an invented number is returned.
detail.whyNotFixed: Doing 32 of these by hand is roughly 32 times the work of doing one, because nothing carries over. And the two rules that matter most — every figure sourced, every gap declared — are exactly the two things that break down when a tired person is finishing their fourth deck.
detail.whatExists:
SELCO has commissioned value chain studies of this type before at state level. Those existing decks and reference material are to be shared at kick-off, and they are the best guide to what “good” looks like.

Section 4 of SELCO’s assignment document sets the mandatory ten-section framework. Obtain it before you write a line, because it defines the output and cannot be restructured.

Only five of the 19 non-priority value chains have been named so far — tea, oranges, jackfruit, ginger and chilli. The urban and disability-related chains are all still unnamed.

Programme duration and the four deliverable dates are placeholders in SELCO’s document. Pin them down at kick-off.
detail.whatYouHave:
- public government, NABARD, SFAC, ICAR, commodity board and state department publications — all openly available
- SELCO’s prior state-level value chain decks and reference material, promised at kick-off
- the ten-section framework and a named reviewer at SELCO. Without both you cannot start drafting
detail.doneIn90Days:
**An important note first.** SELCO wrote this as a research assignment: interns write decks, SELCO reviews them. As written it does not fit this programme, because there is no approach for a team to propose and nothing for a sponsor to choose between, and the output is a set of PowerPoints that shows little of your engineering ability.

The version in this brief reframes it as a tooling problem, which needs SELCO’s agreement before it runs. Under the reframe you deliver both:

- a working pipeline that helps produce these documents — finding and retrieving relevant published sources, pulling figures into the fixed ten-section structure, attaching a citation to every number it carries, and flagging a section as a gap when it cannot find a sourced figure
- three finished value chain decks produced using it, meeting SELCO’s quality standard in full

Across roughly ten teams that produces the priority chains and a tool SELCO keeps.
detail.rules:
- every figure, cost, yield, price and claim carries a named source with a link or full citation. An unsourced number is a defect
- a missing figure is reported as a gap. An invented one gets the draft returned. SELCO’s own words: an honest gap is a useful finding
- indicative costs carry the year as well as the source, because equipment prices date quickly
- content is written in your own words. Copied text is not accepted
- data gaps and scope questions are raised in the first week, not at the end
- final output is PowerPoint and PDF, with a source list appended to each deck

These rules also define your tool. A pipeline that produces fluent text without a traceable source has automated the one thing SELCO will reject.
detail.findingYourApproach:
The temptation is to point a language model at the web and generate decks. That fails SELCO’s review, because a model will produce a confident yield figure for turmeric in Odisha with nothing behind it and no way to tell it from a real one.

The problem worth solving is the inverse of generation. Build something that refuses to state a number it cannot cite, and that treats “no data found” as a correct output rather than a failure.
detail.sponsor:
SELCO Foundation, Innovation Team. Engaged through Sushma at Xcelerator. Assignment issued 5 September 2026.
