- **Branch** — CS, IT. Open to any branch for the research side, since the subject matter spans agriculture, animal husbandry, textiles and small business.
- **Technical skills** — Information retrieval, document parsing and extraction, citation tracking, working with language models under a factual-accuracy constraint, automated document generation.
- **Other skills** — Desk research at a professional standard, judging source credibility, writing to a fixed structure, working to a review cycle with external deadlines.

problems.title: Practising on a Student Who Is Not Real
problems.summary: Facilitator training costs a full day of travel every week. Simulate the student instead.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Project SparkL, described in Brief 06. It works with underprivileged children, many of whom have run away from home, who are placed in a school grade because of their age rather than what they can do. SparkL’s facilitators spend the hours after school closing that gap.

A detail that matters: a child’s grade hides the fact that their reading comprehension, their writing and their reasoning can all be at different levels.
detail.situation:
SparkL has the design, the curriculum and the facilitators. All of it is offline and manual.

Every week, every facilitator travels to one location and spends a full day being trained. The founders spend that day with them — teaching, going through feedback, and analysing what happened in the sessions. That day is where the quality comes from.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The facilitator is the product. Quality control at the facilitator level is the single thing that makes SparkL work, and it currently requires the founders in a room once a week.

So growth costs founder-days, and there are only so many of those. Seven centres is roughly where that ceiling sits.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Because recorded training does not build this skill. Teaching a child who has run away from home, who is nine and cannot count, and who may not want to be there, is a practised interaction. You cannot learn it from a video any more than you can learn to swim from one.

There is a second reason people miss. That weekly day runs in both directions. Training goes down to the facilitators, and feedback and analysis come back up to the founders. A platform that only pushes content downward removes half of what the day does.
detail.whatExists:
SparkL’s curriculum and pedagogy. These are the organisation’s most valuable asset and they are the input your system depends on entirely. Without them you cannot judge good teaching from bad, and everything below falls apart.

Outside SparkL, this has been tried before and you should read it. Mixed-reality classroom simulators, where trainee teachers practise on student avatars, have been used in American teacher education for over a decade — TeachLivE and Mursion are the two best documented, and a scoping review of the field was published in the CITE Journal in 2026. Separately, simulating students with language models has become an active research area, including a classroom-simulation paper at NAACL 2025 and a full review of the architectures involved published in November 2025.

The curriculum and pedagogy documents, the structure of the training day, how many facilitators there are, and what the founders actually assess them on. Get these first. Without them you have no way to tell good teaching from bad, and the project has no ground truth.
detail.whatYouHave:
- the founders, who run the training day and can tell you what they are watching for
- the facilitators themselves, who are the users
- a training day to sit in on. Arranging that is the most useful thing you could do in week one
- recordings or notes from past sessions, if any exist and SparkL will share them
detail.doneIn90Days:
Something a facilitator used, that a founder watched, and that the founder judged to be worth the time.

SparkL and Xcelerator have already discussed one idea for this: an AI avatar that plays a learner. The facilitator teaches it, and it responds like a child in that situation — starting out not knowing the number system, and appearing to learn as the facilitator applies SparkL’s methods. The avatar can be configured for different circumstances and different kinds of learning difficulty.

Treat that as one promising idea, not as the specification. The outcome SparkL needs is that facilitator quality holds up without the founders in the room every week. If you can achieve that another way, propose it.
detail.rules:
- **The avatar must be able to fail to learn.** If it improves no matter what the facilitator does, it teaches nothing and is worse than useless, because it rewards bad practice
- what counts as good teaching comes from SparkL’s pedagogy, not from your judgement or the model’s
- no data about a real child goes into a model or a third-party service
- works in Kannada as well as English, on a modest device and a poor connection
- these are children with difficult histories. Do not build scenarios that simulate distress or trauma for adults to practise on, unless SparkL explicitly designs them and supervises their use
- keep the upward path: what a facilitator does on the platform must reach the founders as feedback
detail.findingYourApproach:
A chatbot told to act like a nine-year-old who cannot count demonstrates beautifully for four minutes and then falls apart. Understand why before you propose anything.

The model already knows arithmetic and drifts back to competence under pressure. It is agreeable, so it will appear to learn from bad teaching, which makes it worse than no tool at all. And real children fail in patterned ways: reciting numbers without understanding quantity, getting it right on Tuesday and wrong on Thursday, guessing what the adult wants instead of thinking.

The team that makes the avatar refuse to learn when taught badly, and can say where that judgement comes from, has the strongest pitch here.
detail.sponsor:
Project SparkL founders. This is their third problem in the pool alongside Briefs 06 and 07.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS, IT. The most demanding language-model problem in this pool, and not a wrapper exercise.
- **Technical skills** — Controlling and constraining model behaviour, evaluation design for open-ended systems, conversation and dialogue design, state modelling, offline and low-bandwidth delivery, Kannada language handling.
- **Other skills** — Understanding pedagogy before automating it, designing a training experience, measuring whether a person actually got better, working with vulnerable-group safeguarding.

problems.title: Telling One Elephant from Another
problems.summary: Management questions are about individual animals, not species counts.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Atria Foundation, the charitable arm of Atria Group, described in Brief 12. One of its four pillars is Bio-Diversity, which it describes as promoting harmony across species. Its visible work there so far has been plantation drives.

This problem sits further from that existing work than the Foundation’s other briefs, and it has one hard dependency: identifying individual animals needs a photographic catalogue that somebody has already built. Where that comes from is the first thing to settle.
detail.situation:
Wildlife management asks questions about individuals, not just species. Is one elephant responsible for most of the crop raiding in a valley, or fifty? Is the animal we translocated the one that came back? How many distinct individuals use this corridor?

Right now those questions are answered by researchers who know the animals personally, which does not scale and disappears when they move on.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Without individual identification, conflict data describes a place rather than an animal. That changes what you can do about it. A single repeat individual is a management problem with a specific answer. Fifty animals passing through is a landscape problem with a different one. The data cannot currently tell you which you have.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Some species make this easy. Tigers have stripe patterns that work almost like barcodes. Elephants do not. Identification relies on a combination of features that are harder to read from a photograph: ear fold shape, notches and tears in the ear edge, depigmentation patches, tail and tail-brush condition, body scars, and tusks where present.

There is also a harder statistical problem underneath, which most projects skip. A system that matches every photograph to the closest animal in its catalogue will confidently mislabel an animal it has never seen. Recognising that a new individual is new is the part that matters and the part that is difficult.
detail.whatExists:
Read ElephantBook before you propose anything. It is a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop elephant re-identification system published at ACM COMPASS in 2021 and deployed with the Mara Elephant Project in Kenya. Note the word semi-automated: the researchers who built it kept a person in the loop deliberately.

Your genuine contribution is that it was built for African elephants. Asian elephants are a different identification problem — most females and many males are tuskless, so tusk shape, one of the strongest African cues, largely disappears. That gap is real, defensible and worth a paper.

Whether a photographic catalogue of identified individuals exists anywhere, how large it is, and whether it can be shared. This project lives or dies on that answer, so get it in week one.
detail.whatYouHave:
- photographic data and existing individual identifications from somewhere. This is the difference between a real project and a public-dataset exercise
- Brief 11 works on the same animals by a different method, for a different sponsor. Talk to whoever takes it — there is more overlap than either brief admits
detail.doneIn90Days:
A working re-identification system tested on real photographs, reported honestly. Two numbers matter and most projects only report the first:

- how often it correctly matches a photograph to a known individual
- how often it correctly says “this animal is not in the catalogue”

Plus the workflow around it: how a researcher confirms or rejects a match, and how a new individual gets added.
detail.rules:
- peer-reviewed documentation standard: reproducible method, stated assumptions, honest error rates
- report the failure cases, including which animals it confuses and why
- location data for individual animals is sensitive and can assist poaching. It does not go into a public repository, a public model, or a demo
- a match is a suggestion to a researcher, never an automatic record
detail.findingYourApproach:
Read ElephantBook before you propose anything, and notice that its authors kept a human in the loop when they could have automated it. Work out why.

Then answer what the standard approach hides: what your system does with a blurry photograph of an animal it has never seen, and how few photographs of a new individual are enough.
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation, under its Bio-Diversity pillar.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS and Electronics. Strong computer vision content.
- **Technical skills** — Computer vision and re-identification, metric learning and embeddings, open-set recognition, working with small and imbalanced datasets, human-in-the-loop system design.
- **Other skills** — Reading and building on published research, scientific writing, reporting error honestly, handling sensitive data.

problems.title: Counting What Lives in a Place
problems.summary: Estimate what species live in an area when detection is always imperfect.
skills: Species classification from image or audio

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Atria Foundation, described in Brief 12, under its Bio-Diversity pillar. The Foundation runs plantation drives and describes its aim there as promoting harmony across species. It has no way at present of saying what any of that has done to the life in a place.
detail.situation:
Someone wants to know what species live in a given area — a forest patch, a farm, a stretch of riverbank. That question sits behind conservation planning, environmental clearance, restoration monitoring and corporate biodiversity reporting.

Several methods exist and each sees a different slice:

- **Camera traps** catch ground-dwelling mammals well and miss small, arboreal and nocturnal-silent species
- **Acoustic recorders** catch birds, bats, frogs and insects that call, and miss everything that does not
- **Environmental DNA** detects traces of many species from a water or soil sample, but needs a laboratory, sequencing, and a reference database that is incomplete for Indian species
- **Transect and plot surveys** are reliable and expensive in expert time
- **Citizen records** such as bird and nature-observation platforms are large and heavily biased toward attractive species near roads
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Each method gives you a list that reflects the method as much as the place. Combining them is not addition, because each one detects different species with different probability, so you cannot simply pool the lists and call it a survey.
detail.whyNotFixed: Because it is a genuine open problem in ecology, not an engineering oversight. Estimating how many species are present when your detection is imperfect and varies by method is a live statistical research area. Anyone promising a complete answer is overselling.
detail.whatExists:
Brief 11 covers acoustic species classification with CWS, and an engineering student is already working on that classifier. This problem overlaps with it directly. Whoever takes this must coordinate with that team, or the two will duplicate each other.

A study site, any existing survey data, and access to recording or sampling equipment. Find out what is available before you choose your methods.
detail.whatYouHave:
- public biodiversity databases and citizen-science records, which are freely available
- a real study site, and permission to place equipment on it
- laboratory access if you want to do any DNA work. Without a sequencing arrangement, environmental DNA is not open to you and you should not build a proposal around it
detail.doneIn90Days:
One real place, at least two methods, one defensible estimate with its uncertainty stated. That is a complete and honest project.

What matters is the combination. Showing how two imperfect methods can be joined into an estimate better than either alone, with the assumptions written down, is the contribution. A species list without a stated detection assumption is a list, not a survey.
detail.rules:
- every estimate carries its uncertainty and its detection assumptions
- an absence of records is not evidence of absence, and the output must not imply otherwise
- location records for threatened species are withheld or made deliberately imprecise
- any fieldwork follows the permissions required for the site
detail.findingYourApproach:
Photograph-and-identify platforms already exist and are very good. Rebuilding one is not a contribution.

The opportunity is in the unglamorous middle: taking data that already exists and turning it into an estimate a conservation planner would act on. That means being honest about what each method cannot see.
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation, under its Bio-Diversity pillar.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS and Electronics, with a strong pull for anyone interested in ecology or statistics.
- **Technical skills** — Statistical estimation under imperfect detection, combining heterogeneous data sources, species classification from images or audio, sensor deployment, data visualisation.
- **Other skills** — Reading ecological literature, stating uncertainty, resisting the urge to claim completeness.

problems.title: Getting Coconuts Down
problems.summary: Skilled climbers are scarce and ageing, and the fruit is at the top of a smooth trunk.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Atria Foundation, described in Brief 12. The Foundation’s farm names coconut harvesting as its single biggest operational problem.
detail.situation:
Coconut palms grow tall, with a smooth unbranched trunk and the fruit at the very top. Harvesting means getting a person or a machine up there, cutting bunches, and getting down. Skilled climbers are scarce, ageing, and the work is dangerous.

The farm reports that the robots currently available do not work well on coconuts.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Unharvested or late-harvested coconuts are lost income. Dependence on a shrinking pool of climbers is a risk the farm cannot control. And unlike most farm tasks, this one cannot be solved by simply hiring more people, because the skill takes years to acquire.
detail.whyNotFixed:
It has been attempted seriously, and you should know the numbers before you propose anything.

**Amaran** is an unmanned robotic coconut tree climber and harvester built at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, in development since 2014 under Rajesh Kannan Megalingam and published in IEEE in 2020. A ring-shaped body clasps trunks of varying diameter, eight wheels drive it up and around the trunk, it copes with trunks leaning up to 30 degrees, and a robotic arm with four degrees of freedom cuts the bunches. It is teleoperated by app or joystick and carries a backup battery so it can come down if power fails.

Its measured performance is the most useful fact in this brief. Amaran averages **21.9 minutes per tree, of which about 14 minutes is setup**. That works out to roughly 22 trees a day, against about 15 for a human climber before fatigue. Cost is described as the barrier to wider deployment.

The team’s own summary of the difficulty is worth repeating: no two coconut trees are the same.
detail.whatExists:
Amaran and the published work around it, including more recent double-ring climber designs. Read the papers. A proposal that reinvents a 2020 design without knowing it exists will not survive the scoping round.

The most important question on this brief: which machines has the farm actually tried, and how exactly did they fail? Cost, tree geometry, setup time — or were they never tried at all? The answer changes what you should build, so ask before you design.

Number of palms, height range, trunk lean and diameter, ground conditions between trees, harvest frequency, and current cost per tree. Go and measure.
detail.whatYouHave:
- the Foundation’s own farm, which should be the easiest site access of any problem in this pool
- the people who currently harvest, who know exactly where the time goes
- a workshop, tools and a materials budget, none of which is guaranteed
detail.doneIn90Days:
Something that goes up a real tree on the real farm and brings coconuts down, tested more than once, with three numbers: time per tree against the current method, cost to build one, and how many of the farm’s trees your design can actually handle.

That last number is where most designs quietly fail. A machine that works on a straight 40 cm trunk and cannot manage a leaning one has solved a fraction of the problem.
detail.rules:
- safety first, and this is not a formality. A machine at 20 metres that falls, or a cutting tool that drops, can kill someone. Design the failure case before the working case
- the tree is not damaged. A palm is a long-term asset and injuring the crown can end it
- low cost and locally repairable, since cost is exactly what stopped the existing solutions
- works on the farm’s real range of trunk diameters and leans, not one ideal specimen
detail.findingYourApproach:
Read the Amaran work before you design anything, then look hard at one number in it. Setup takes roughly fourteen of its twenty-two minutes per tree, so only about eight minutes is climbing and cutting.

Making the climb faster barely moves the total. Most teams will optimise the wrong number. Decide which number you are attacking, and say so.
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Mechanical, with Electronics on control and teleoperation. The most demanding mechanical problem in the pool.
- **Technical skills** — Mechanism and gripper design, climbing and traction systems, structural analysis and failure modes, actuators and control, remote operation, safety engineering, cost engineering.
- **Other skills** — Reading prior art properly, measuring where time actually goes, designing for the worst tree rather than the best one.

problems.title: Reading a Plant's Electrical Signals
problems.summary: By the time stress is visible the damage is days old. Catch it in the plant's signals.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Atria Foundation, described in Brief 12. This problem sits across two of its pillars — Bio-Diversity and the farm work behind Brief 22 — and would be tested on the Foundation’s own crops.
detail.situation: By the time a farmer can see that a plant is stressed — wilting, yellowing, stunted growth — the damage has usually been happening for days. Water stress, disease, nutrient deficiency and heat all announce themselves late. Anything that gives warning earlier is worth money and worth water.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Existing early-warning tools measure the environment rather than the plant. Soil moisture sensors tell you about the soil. Weather stations tell you about the air. Neither tells you what the plant is actually experiencing, and two plants in the same soil can be in very different states.
detail.whatExists:
A substantial research literature on plant electrical signalling, including recent reviews and a body of work on electrophysiology for crop production. Commercial plant electrophysiology sensing exists. Low-cost electrode and amplifier designs for plant signals are widely published, so the hardware is within reach of a student budget.

Which site would host an experiment and which crops it grows. Settle both before week three, because the experiment needs a baseline period before anything else can happen.
detail.whatYouHave:
- published research and open hardware designs for plant electrode measurement
- plants, growing space, and the ability to control watering and conditions
- laboratory or greenhouse access, which makes a controlled experiment far easier
detail.doneIn90Days:
A real experiment with a real answer, either way.

- instrument a set of plants of one species, with a control group kept healthy
- apply one known, controlled stress — withholding water is the easiest to do properly
- record electrical signals continuously, and record visible condition separately
- report whether the signal distinguished stressed from healthy plants, and crucially **how long before the stress became visible**

That last number is the entire value of the project. If the signal tells you two days early, you have something a farmer would use. If it tells you at the same moment the leaves droop, you have proved something useful and negative.
detail.rules:
- a control group is required. Without unstressed plants measured the same way, you have no result
- any claim about health carries the number of plants, the effect size and how confident you are
- sonification, if you build it, is presented as an output. It is never offered as evidence
- a negative result reported clearly is a successful project. Manufacturing a positive one is not
- no claims about plant consciousness, emotion, communication or preference. None of these follow from an electrical measurement
detail.findingYourApproach:
A device that clips onto a plant and plays generative music will look and sound wonderful, and will tell nobody anything about the plant.

Start from the experiment and treat the hardware as the means. If your proposal names what you will measure, against what control, and what result would prove you wrong, you are ahead of almost every team on this problem.
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Electronics primarily, with CS for the analysis. Genuine instrumentation and signal processing content.
- **Technical skills** — Biopotential measurement, electrode design, low-noise amplification, signal processing, time-series classification, experimental design and statistics.
- **Other skills** — Designing an experiment that can disprove your own hypothesis, reading scientific literature critically, separating a real effect from a compelling demonstration.

problems.title: The Gap Between Knowing and Doing
problems.summary: Young adults know what would help their wellbeing and still do not do it. Measure what closes the gap.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
InspireMinds works on behaviour change in young people, using games, stories, yoga, reflection and design thinking rather than lectures. Its method runs Learn, Experience, Reflect, Apply, Grow.

It has a real product suite: four illustrated books — CricketYogi teaches the eight limbs of yoga through cricket, Happy Yogi covers nervous-system regulation, Yogic Science links anatomy to sustainability, Wealthy Yogi builds money habits — plus a nutrition game and Swadhyaya, a 21-day self-inquiry journal. It reports reaching more than 2,500 children across 7 or more states.
detail.situation:
All of that is built for children. InspireMinds now wants to work with colleges, and young adults are a different problem.

The need is real. InspireMinds cites Deloitte’s 2025 Gen Z and Millennial Survey, which found that 94% of Gen Z respondents in India rate on-the-job learning as the most impactful thing for career progression, and reports that a third of Indian Gen Z respondents experience frequent stress or anxiety during their studies.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Two things, and the second is the more interesting one.

First, a nineteen-year-old will not engage with a picture book written for a ten-year-old. The method may transfer to college students. The material does not.

Second, and this is the real opening: **InspireMinds cannot yet show that behaviour changed.** Its strongest reported figures are that 91% gained the intended nutritional and wellness knowledge and 87% learned more than two food or nutrient concepts. Read those carefully. Both measure what someone *knows* after a session.

InspireMinds’ own first principle is that children can know what is right and still not do it. So its evidence measures the thing it says is not the problem. Closing that gap — showing a real, observed change in what people actually do — is the most valuable thing a student team could build for this organisation.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Because measuring behaviour is much harder than measuring knowledge, and much harder than it looks.

- people over-report good habits and under-report bad ones, so asking them is not enough
- almost any intervention works for three weeks. Novelty alone produces a result, and the interesting question is week seven
- campus life fights you: irregular timetables, exam cycles, peer norms and hostel routines all overwhelm an individual’s intentions
- observing behaviour without surveilling people is a genuine design constraint, not a formality
detail.whatExists:
The product suite, the five-stage pathway, and the pilot results above.

InspireMinds has also proposed a complete format for working with colleges — the Personal Growth Innovation Challenge, where each student picks a personal goal, diagnoses their own gap, and engineers a fix. It is thoughtfully designed. It is also a description of a competition rather than a problem to solve, so this brief takes the organisational need underneath it instead. See section 07.

The product materials, and the pilot data behind the 91% and 87% figures — how they were measured, and on how many people. Ask for both. The second one tells you what InspireMinds can and cannot currently prove.
detail.whatYouHave:
- InspireMinds’ behavioural frameworks, curriculum toolkits and facilitation, all of which they have offered
- a study population sitting on your own campus, which no other brief in this pool has
- a campus cohort, a room and a timetable slot, and a way of recruiting participants. All of it is yours to organise
- a facilitation session from InspireMinds during your cycle, if you ask for one
- whoever at Atria approves a study involving students as participants. Find them in week one, because nothing can run without them
detail.doneIn90Days:
**An important note first.** InspireMinds pitched a campus challenge in which every student picks their own personal goal. That format cannot run inside this programme: with around nine teams each pursuing a different self-chosen goal, there is nothing comparable for a sponsor to greenlight, nothing to hand over at the end, and the evidence a student would carry away is a claim about themselves.

The version in this brief keeps InspireMinds’ real need and needs their agreement: **design an intervention that changes one specific behaviour in 18 to 22 year olds, run it on a real campus cohort, and measure honestly whether it worked.** Every team then attacks the same target from a different angle, InspireMinds can choose between the approaches, and the winning intervention becomes part of their college offering.

Choose one behaviour and name it precisely. Sleep timing. Screen use after midnight. Eating breakfast. Exercise three times a week. One.

Deliver: the intervention, a measured before-and-after with a comparison or baseline period, and a plain statement of what happened.
detail.rules:
- **measure behaviour, not knowledge and not intention.** What someone learned, or plans to do, is not a result
- self-report alone is not enough. Pair it with something observable
- you need a baseline period or a comparison group. Without one you cannot claim anything
- every participant consents, knows they can stop, and is never identifiable in what you hand over. They are your classmates, so the pressure to take part is real and you must design it out
- stay out of clinical territory. If a participant discloses serious distress, you must have a route to a real person who can help, not a form and not a chatbot
- **report what actually happened.** An intervention that did not work, reported clearly, is a successful project. Manufacturing a positive result is the one failure that matters here
- you do not diagnose or screen anyone
detail.findingYourApproach:
There are thousands of habit trackers and their documented problem is that people stop opening them. Assume yours will too, unless you can say why not.

Two questions decide whether a pitch is serious. What makes someone do the thing on day forty, when the novelty has gone and nobody is watching? And how do you know they did it, without taking their word for it and without following them around?
detail.sponsor:
InspireMinds.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS and IT for the intervention and data, Electronics for sensing and wearables. Open to any branch with an interest in behavioural science or statistics.
- **Technical skills** — Experiment design, measurement instrumentation, mobile and wearable data capture, time-series and statistical analysis, privacy-preserving data handling, interface design for daily use.
- **Other skills** — Research ethics and consent, running a study with human participants, recruiting and retaining them, reporting a result that disappoints the sponsor.

problems.title: Ten Rupees a Ride
problems.summary: Mobile signal along a railway line drops out for long stretches. Serve the passenger anyway.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Atria Foundation, described in Brief 12. This is one of a group of problems the Foundation has put forward that sit outside its four existing pillars.

Be aware that the brief is built on one paragraph of intent. Almost everything below the situation is yours to establish.
detail.situation:
Indian Railways moves roughly 23 million passengers a day. A long-distance journey runs for hours. A suburban commute runs twice a day, every day, for years.

Mobile signal along a railway line is patchy and drops out entirely for long stretches. So passengers either download something before they board, or stare out of the window.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
Nothing is broken. This is an opportunity that nobody has taken at a price ordinary passengers would pay.

The target set for you is ten rupees per person per ride. That number is the whole problem. It rules out almost every business model that works elsewhere, and it is low enough that a passenger might actually pay it without thinking.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Two reasons, and only one of them is technical.

The technical one is that you cannot stream from the internet on a moving train, so content has to already be on board. Then one server has to serve hundreds of phones at once over wireless, in a metal tube, while everyone is watching something different. Wireless capacity, not storage, is what breaks first.

The commercial one is harder. At ten rupees a head you cannot license premium film content. The rights alone would eat the fare several times over. Indian Railways has announced its own on-demand video, news and multilingual content on trains, and edge-cached video for rail operators is already a commercial product internationally, so you would not be first.
detail.whatExists:
Railway station wireless networks, Indian Railways’ own announced onboard entertainment, and international rail streaming products that cache content at the edge. Find out what each of them charges and what content they carry before you assume there is a gap.

Whether the Foundation has any relationship with a railway operator, and whether this has been discussed with anyone at Indian Railways, is for you to find out.
detail.whatYouHave:
- your own hardware and a coach-sized space to simulate in, since a real train is unlikely to be available to you
- access to a train, a depot or a railway operator, if you can get it. Without one this is a laboratory project — a legitimate outcome, but a different one
detail.doneIn90Days:
A working system serving many devices at once from a local cache with no internet, and a costed argument that the whole thing survives at ten rupees a head.

The demonstration matters less than the number. Show how many simultaneous viewers one unit supports, what it costs to build and run, what content it could legally carry at that price, and how many passengers would have to buy for it to pay for itself.

Test at real scale. Thirty phones in a room is a result. Three is not.
detail.rules:
- no content is distributed without the right to distribute it. A system that only works by ignoring copyright is not a system
- the design assumes no internet on board, not slow internet
- nothing is proposed for installation on rolling stock without acknowledging that railway equipment needs operator approval and certification
- the ten rupee figure is a constraint to be tested, not an assumption to be quietly dropped. If your model only works at fifty rupees, say so and show the arithmetic
detail.findingYourApproach:
Most teams will treat this as a streaming problem and build a media server. That part is close to a solved problem, and it will not distinguish you.

The questions that decide it: how many phones can one wireless access point actually serve before the video stutters, and what changes if everyone watches the same thing at the same time rather than different things? What content can you lawfully carry for ten rupees a head, and who would want it? And who pays — the passenger, an advertiser, or the operator?
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — Electronics for the wireless and hardware side, CS and IT for the software and the caching. One of the more balanced problems in this pool.
- **Technical skills** — Wireless networking and capacity planning, local caching and content delivery, adaptive streaming, embedded and low-power hardware, load testing at realistic scale.
- **Other skills** — Unit economics, content licensing basics, reading a regulated environment, testing a claim rather than demonstrating a feature.

problems.title: Work After Sixty
problems.summary: People retire at 58 to 60 with decades of skill left. Match them to work that wants it.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
Atria Foundation, described in Brief 12. Its Education pillar already runs skilling and placement through the Atria Mega Skill Centre, which has trained over 4,000 people and placed around 620 with employers. That is the same shape of problem at the other end of a working life.

As with Brief 25, the brief is built on one paragraph of intent. Establish the rest yourself.
detail.situation:
People in India’s organised sector typically retire around 58 to 60, and then live for decades. Many of them are highly skilled, have run teams, solved problems and know an industry from the inside.

Some want to keep working. Not all of them on the old terms: fewer hours, no commute, no travel, something that fits around health or caring for a spouse.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: That experience mostly goes unused. The people who want work cannot find the right work, and the constraints they come with — part-time, remote, flexible, no heavy travel — are exactly the ones ordinary job platforms handle worst.
detail.whatExists:
Several Indian job portals aimed at retired people and the over-sixties. Treat them as your literature review, not your competition.

Whether the Foundation can open a group of retired people, or its Skill Centre employer relationships, to you. Ask early: the employer side is the hard half.
detail.whatYouHave:
- retired people you can talk to, who are not hard to find and who will tell you things a survey never would
- the Foundation’s existing employer relationships through the Skill Centre, if they can be opened to you
- an employer willing to take part in a trial during your cycle. Finding one is arguably the project
detail.doneIn90Days:
Evidence about the demand side, and something built on top of it.

The strongest possible outcome is small and real: a handful of genuine matches that happened, with the story of what made each employer say yes. Ten real placements beats a platform with a thousand registered profiles and no vacancies.

If you conclude the platform is not the answer, say so and show what is. That is a finding, not a failure.
detail.rules:
- talk to employers in the first two weeks. A team that has only spoken to retirees by week six has built on the easy side of the market
- no personal data about any individual is published or shared without their clear agreement
- no promise of work to anyone during a student project. Raising the hopes of someone looking for income is a real harm
- design around the constraints people actually state, not the ones you assume older people have
detail.findingYourApproach:
A profile database with a matching algorithm is where almost every team will start, and it is the thing that has already been built several times.

Two questions decide whether your pitch is serious. Where does the demand come from — what makes an employer post a role they would not otherwise have posted? And what is the smallest version of this that could produce one real match inside your cycle, so you find out whether any of it is true?
detail.sponsor:
Atria Foundation.

The programme team will put you in touch and set up the first conversation.
detail.skillsAndBranches:
- **Branch** — CS and IT. Suits students who want product and research work more than heavy engineering.
- **Technical skills** — Matching and recommendation logic, accessible interface design for older users, lightweight backend, privacy-aware data handling.
- **Other skills** — Interviewing on both sides of a market, testing a demand assumption before building, accessibility, reporting a conclusion the sponsor did not expect.

problems.title: Beyond the Bin: eco food packaging

detail.situation: Food packaging is widely used to protect and transport food, but many conventional materials are made from plastics or other non-biodegradable materials.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Conventional packaging generates large amounts of waste and can remain in the environment for a long time. Many sustainable alternatives may also have limitations in strength, durability, water resistance, cost, or food safety.
detail.whyNotFixed: Developing a sustainable material that is biodegradable, safe for food contact, strong, lightweight, and affordable is technically challenging. Existing alternatives may not satisfy all these requirements at the same time.

detail.whatYouHave: We would work with biodegradable or renewable raw materials, natural fibers, agricultural waste, biopolymers, and other suitable materials. We would also need basic laboratory equipment and testing methods to prepare and evaluate the packaging material.

detail.rules:

- The material should be biodegradable or environmentally sustainable and should minimize plastic waste.

- Food safety and hygiene requirements must not be compromised during material preparation or testing.

- The developed material should have sufficient strength and durability for its intended packaging use.

problems.title: Farmer decision platform
problems.summary: Crop, weather, scheme and market information is fragmented across sources.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: The project would primarily work with small and marginal farmers and other members of the local agricultural community. The team would also interact with agricultural experts, field workers, NGOs or community organizations, and other stakeholders who can provide practical insights into farming-related problems. Where relevant, the project may also consider interactions with agricultural equipment owners, buyers, and other participants involved in the agricultural supply chain. Their feedback will help the team understand actual farmer requirements and ensure that the proposed platform is designed around practical needs rather than only technical assumptions.
detail.situation: Farmers make several important decisions throughout the farming cycle, from selecting a suitable crop and preparing the soil to managing weather risks, diseases, harvesting, and selling the produce. However, access to reliable and timely agricultural information is not always easy, particularly for farmers with limited digital literacy or limited access to agricultural advisory services.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Farmers may face difficulties in selecting crops according to their soil, climate, season, and local conditions. Unpredictable weather can affect sowing, irrigation, crop growth, and harvesting. Crop diseases and pests can also result in crop losses when they are not identified and managed at an early stage. In addition, farmers may not always have easy access to current information about market prices, demand, potential buyers, or agricultural machinery. These challenges become more difficult when information is available through multiple disconnected sources or is presented in a way that is difficult for farmers to understand and use. As a result, farmers may have difficulty making timely and informed decisions throughout the farming cycle.
detail.whyNotFixed: Existing agricultural services and digital platforms often address individual needs such as weather information, crop advisory, market prices, or disease identification.The challenge is bringing these different requirements together in a simple, localized, and farmer-friendly system that can support decision-making across multiple stages of farming.
detail.whatExists: There are existing agricultural websites, mobile applications, weather services, market information systems, and crop advisory platforms. Our project will study these existing solutions and identify gaps in usability, integration, localization, and accessibility rather than attempting to duplicate services that already work effectively.
detail.whatYouHave: The project will build upon the existing Khet prototype developed during the earlier IDT project and extend it as part of ASIP. The team will work with the knowledge and observations collected during the GKVK field visit, agricultural resources, publicly available agricultural information, user feedback, and suitable technology for developing the platform. The existing prototype provides a starting point for the project, while the ASIP phase will focus on validating actual farmer requirements and improving the platform accordingly. The proposed platform may include crop recommendation, crop and soil information, weather updates, disease identification support, market information, farming guidance, multilingual support, and other features based on validated user needs and project feasibility.
detail.findingYourApproach:
The team will follow a user-centered and iterative approach. The first stage will involve understanding and validating farmer problems through field interaction, stakeholder discussions, and requirement analysis. Based on the collected information, the team will prioritize the most relevant problems and identify features that can provide practical value. The existing Khet prototype will then be improved based on these findings. The development process will include designing the user interface, implementing selected features, testing the prototype with potential users, collecting feedback, identifying usability issues, and making necessary improvements. The overall approach will focus on developing a practical and accessible solution rather than attempting to implement every proposed feature at once.

problems.title: Surplus food redistribution
problems.summary: Surplus food and hunger exist a few kilometres apart. The routing between them is the problem.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: We would work with restaurants, hotels, college canteens, hostels, supermarkets, event organizers, NGOs, volunteers, and organizations involved in collecting and distributing surplus food.
detail.situation:
Large quantities of edible food are prepared every day in restaurants, hotels, college canteens, hostels, functions, supermarkets, and households. A portion of this food remains unused because of overproduction, inaccurate demand estimation, cancellations, unsold inventory, or changes in customer demand.

At the same time, many people and communities face difficulty accessing sufficient food. Although food-delivery platforms have made food easily accessible, there is still no widely integrated system that efficiently identifies surplus food, determines whether it is safe to distribute, and connects it with nearby organizations or people who can use it.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The current food ecosystem has several gaps.

First, food providers often do not know how much food will actually be required, resulting in overproduction. Second, surplus food is frequently identified manually and may not reach an organization quickly enough before its safe consumption window expires.

Third, there is no simple centralized system connecting food donors, NGOs, volunteers, and recipients in real time. Information such as quantity, food type, preparation time, expiry/safe-consumption window, pickup location, and availability may be scattered across phone calls or messaging applications.

This results in edible food being discarded while potentially useful food remains inaccessible to people who need it.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Existing food-delivery and inventory systems mainly focus on selling food and managing commercial orders rather than managing surplus food after it becomes available.

Some food donation initiatives operate through manual coordination, but they can face challenges such as delayed communication, inaccurate quantity information, transportation limitations, food-safety verification, and difficulty matching available food with the nearest suitable recipient organization.

A complete solution requires combining AI-based demand prediction, surplus detection, inventory tracking, food-safety information, location-based matching, and volunteer coordination into one lightweight platform.
detail.whatExists:
Existing technologies include food-delivery applications, inventory-management systems, GPS/location services, database systems, machine-learning prediction algorithms, QR codes, and NGO donation platforms.

However, these technologies are generally not integrated into a single system specifically designed to predict food requirements, identify surplus food, prioritize redistribution, and coordinate its collection before the food becomes unusable.
detail.whatYouHave:
A primarily software-based environment built using Python and free/open-source technologies.

The system can use synthetic food inventory and demand data for initial development and testing. The application can simulate restaurants, canteens, supermarkets, NGOs, volunteers, and food recipients without requiring physical food-distribution infrastructure during the prototype phase.

Possible technologies include:

Python

Streamlit

Pandas

NumPy

Scikit-Learn

SQLite

FPDF2

OpenStreetMap-based offline/sample location data where appropriate
detail.findingYourApproach:
The application will be divided into independent modules.

A Food Provider Module will allow restaurants, canteens, hotels, supermarkets, and event organizers to enter available food, quantity, preparation time, and estimated safe-consumption period.

An AI Demand Prediction Module will analyse historical consumption patterns and predict approximate future food requirements, helping providers reduce overproduction.

A Surplus Detection Module will identify food that is likely to remain unused based on available quantity, predicted demand, and time remaining.

A Smart Matching Module will match available surplus food with suitable nearby NGOs or distribution partners based on food quantity, food category, location, and urgency.

A Volunteer Coordination Module can generate pickup tasks and prioritize food based on remaining safe-consumption time.

A Food Safety Module will record preparation time, storage conditions entered by the user, and recommended action status. The system will flag entries requiring human verification rather than independently declaring food safe.

An Analytics Dashboard will display estimated food saved, quantity redistributed, number of donation events, estimated waste prevented, and participating organizations.

Finally, a PDF Report Module will generate downloadable reports containing donation, collection, redistribution, and impact information.
detail.rules:
○ Software-First Architecture

The initial prototype must be developed primarily as a software system. Physical sensors, smart packaging, or specialized hardware are not mandatory for the first version.

○ Low-Compute Optimization

The system must be optimized to operate on standard consumer laptops. Heavy deep-learning models requiring dedicated GPUs should not be necessary for the prototype.

○ Privacy and Responsible Data Handling

The system should avoid collecting unnecessary personal information about food recipients. Sensitive information should not be exposed through the public dashboard.

○ Food-Safety Limitation

The application must not independently certify food as safe for human consumption. It can record user-provided information, calculate time-based indicators, and flag food for verification by responsible personnel.

○ Simulation-Based Validation

During the prototype stage, testing can be performed using synthetic datasets representing food quantities, demand, locations, preparation times, and donation requests.

○ Human Verification

Final decisions regarding food safety, collection, and distribution should remain with authorized food providers, NGOs, volunteers, or responsible personnel.

problems.title: Air-defence monitoring console
problems.summary: Detect GPS spoofing and predict curving drone trajectories on one operator console.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: We would work with system operators and monitoring staff at ground radar stations who watch border airspace maps for unusual movements.
detail.situation: Ground monitoring stations receive continuous streams of coordinate data (latitude and longitude strings) from radar equipment. Operators use software dashboards to map out these positions visually and spot incoming threats early.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Current monitoring setups face two critical problems. First, enemy electronic warfare can send fake coordinate data (GPS Spoofing) to the radar screen, showing fake aircraft that do not exist. Second, modern drones fly in curves and zig-zag lines to escape, but traditional tracking software assumes they only fly in straight lines, causing operators to...
detail.whyNotFixed: Existing industrial air defense platforms (like the macro-level IACCS framework) are built for heavy server infrastructure and focus heavily on straight-line, long-range heavy aircraft. They require heavy computing hardware and often do not isolate edge-spoofing vectors at the ingestion source level. Furthermore, deep-learning models require expensive graphics processing units (GPUs) that are not available at rural field stations.
detail.whatExists: Standard open-source geospatial frameworks (like Python Streamlit and Leaflet maps), statistical machine learning toolkits (Scikit-Learn Regression packages), and standard vector geometry algorithms for signal localization.
detail.whatYouHave: A 100% software environment built entirely in Python. We do not have real drones or radar devices. We will use a Python script that generates a simulated stream of moving coordinate pairs (numbers) to act as our fake drone data. We will use free, open-source libraries: Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-Learn, and FPDF2.
detail.findingYourApproach: We will split the application into independent code modules. A background loop creates a moving target coordinate list. A security script measures its speed; if it teleports too fast, a cyber alarm triggers. Safe coordinates pass to a simple curve-fitting machine learning function to forecast the next 5 movement points. A separate tab uses circle geometry to intersect radio tower reports, and a PDF writer converts the text tables into a downloadable summary document.
detail.rules:
100% Python-Based Architecture:

The entire platform must be coded exclusively in Python. The use of external web languages like HTML, CSS, or JavaScript is restricted to ensure smooth code integration across all team modules.

○ Low-Compute CPU Optimization:

The system must be optimized to run efficiently on standard consumer laptops. It is restricted from using heavy deep-learning networks that require specialized hardware or dedicated graphics cards (GPUs).

○ Air-Gapped Offline Operation:

In compliance with military security protocols, the application must function completely offline. It cannot rely on active internet connections, cloud databases, or external mapping APIs.

○ Simulation-Based Validation:

The project is strictly software-defined. System testing and evaluation trials will be conducted entirely through an internal synthetic data generator, removing any requirement for physical hardware or real drone assets.
detail.doneIn90Days: During the initial 90-day phase of this multi-semester project, the core focus is on foundational competence training, data protocol definition, and isolated component prototyping. By Day 90, the project will achieve successful milestone completion when all team members complete technical self-study modules across their respective Python frameworks (Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-Learn, and FPDF2). Concurrently, the team will deliver functioning, independent backend code scripts verified via terminal compilation. These artifacts will include a background telemetry pipeline that structures simulated spatial coordinates at precise time intervals, an automated mathematical validation loop that flags anomalous velocity thresholds for the cybersecurity layer, a localized regression script that outputs single-step predictive trajectories, and a static web-based interface wireframe establishing the core dashboard layout

problems.title: Mine subsidence early warning
problems.summary: Low-cost real-time monitoring and warning for ground subsidence over underground coal mines.

detail.whoYouWorkWith:
The project would involve collaboration with underground mine operators, mining engineers, mine safety officers, geologists, geotechnical engineers, mine surveyors, electrical/IoT engineers, AI/ML developers and GIS specialists. The system would also need inputs from personnel responsible for mine planning and emergency response so that alerts generated by the system can support practical operational decisions.

Where feasible, interaction with communities living near underground mining areas would also help understand the practical impact of subsidence, the warning mechanisms currently available to them, and the type of alerts that would be most useful during a potential ground-instability event.
detail.situation:
Underground coal extraction can create changes in the stress and stability of the overlying rock and soil layers. In some locations, these changes can eventually result in surface deformation or subsidence, affecting nearby communities, roads, buildings, agricultural land, forests and other infrastructure.

The problem statement identifies that subsidence monitoring in India is still largely dependent on conventional field observations, periodic surveys and post-facto damage assessments, which may not provide sufficiently timely warning before a critical ground-failure event.

A safer approach requires continuous observation of small changes in the ground before they develop into a more serious event. This creates a need for a low-cost system that can collect measurements continuously from multiple locations, analyze the data automatically and communicate warnings to responsible personnel.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong:
The main issue is that ground deformation can develop progressively, while monitoring may not always be continuous or spatially dense enough to identify every early-stage change.

Important indicators such as:

- abnormal ground tilt,

- changes in relative distance between monitoring points,

- early crack formation,

- unusual vibration patterns

may provide useful evidence of developing instability. The problem specifically identifies these parameters as signals that the proposed system should continuously monitor.

The lack of a unified real-time system can also make it difficult to combine sensor measurements, historical information, spatial information and AI-based analysis into one operational view.
detail.whyNotFixed:
Mine subsidence is a complex engineering problem because conditions vary from mine to mine depending on geology, mining methods, underground panel layout, depth, ground characteristics and environmental conditions.

A practical solution also needs to satisfy several requirements simultaneously:

low cost + continuous sensing + low power operation + reliable communication + accurate anomaly detection + spatial visualization + actionable alerts.

A system designed for underground coal mines cannot simply depend on a single sensor or a generic machine-learning model. It needs multiple sensing points and should be robust enough to operate under Indian geo-mining conditions, therefore calls for a solution that is robust, low power, scalable and suitable for Indian geo-mining conditions.
detail.whatExists:
Current approaches include conventional field observations, periodic surveys and post-facto damage assessment. The problem also envisages the use of technologies such as tilt/inclination sensors, vibration sensors, displacement/stretch sensors, crack-detection sensors and positioning modules, connected through wireless communication networks such as LoRa, Zigbee or Wi-Fi mesh.

The proposed project would build on these existing sensing and surveying approaches rather than completely replacing formal mining and geotechnical assessment. Its focus would be on adding a continuous, distributed and AI-assisted monitoring layer that can detect abnormal patterns, estimate risk and generate early warnings.

The expected solution also includes AI/ML-based anomaly detection, subsidence prediction, GIS-based risk visualization, automated alerts, interactive dashboards, offline capability and scalable deployment.

- vibration sensor

- crack detection mechanism

- optional GPS/GNSS or other positioning module

- LoRa or another suitable wireless communication method

- gateway for collecting sensor data

problems.title: Rain Guard newspaper carrier
problems.summary: Papers are delivered by bicycle and scooter before dawn, through the monsoon.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: We would work directly with local newspaper distributors and vendors who deliver papers on bicycles and scooters during early morning hours, along with newspaper distribution agencies and vendor associations who can connect us to the wider distributor community. Local hardware and fabrication vendors would support prototyping, and faculty mentors would guide the technical design and testing process.
detail.situation: India has one of the largest print media markets in the world, with over 330 million daily newspaper readers. Supporting this ecosystem is a vast network of more than 500,000 newspaper distributors, most of whom operate at the grassroots level using bicycles or scooters to deliver papers during early morning hours, typically between 4 AM and 6 AM. These distributors form the last-mile backbone of print media delivery in India.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Their work is severely disrupted during the monsoon season, which affects large parts of the country for nearly five to six months every year. Sudden and unpredictable early morning rainfall causes newspapers to become wet and unreadable before they reach the customer. Since distributors carry bundles of 50 to 80 papers at a time with minimal protective covering, even a brief rain shower can damage an entire batch, resulting in direct financial loss for the distributor.
detail.whyNotFixed: This problem disproportionately affects economically vulnerable workers who depend entirely on daily delivery completion for their livelihood. There exists no affordable, scalable, or technology-driven solution designed specifically for this segment of workers.
detail.whatExists: The current solutions adopted by distributors are entirely manual. Most use a loose plastic sheet to cover their bundle, which is ineffective during heavy rainfall and difficult to deploy quickly while riding in the dark. In cases of very heavy rain, distributors are forced to skip entire delivery routes, leading to customer dissatisfaction, subscription cancellations, and loss of daily income for an already low-margin occupation.
detail.whatYouHave: It is a limited prototyping budget for materials such as rain sensors, a small motor/actuator, waterproof fabric, and a mounting frame for bicycles and scooters. Access to a small group of local newspaper distributors for feedback and field testing, along with faculty mentorship and basic electronics/fabrication workshop facilities.
detail.findingYourApproach: This project aims to address this gap by designing a smart, portable, weatherproof newspaper carrier system with automatic rain detection and motorized protection, built specifically for use on bicycles and scooters, and priced within reach of the distributor community it serves.
detail.rules: The device must be lightweight and compact enough to mount on a standard bicycle or scooter without affecting the rider's balance or visibility. It must be priced within reach of a low-margin distributor's income, operate reliably in low-light, early-morning conditions, and be quick and simple to deploy without slowing down the delivery route.
detail.doneIn90Days: A working prototype of the Rain Guard carrier, mounted on a bicycle or scooter, that automatically detects rain and deploys motorized weatherproof protection over a bundle of 50 to 80 newspapers. The prototype will have been field-tested with a small group of real distributors, refined based on their feedback, and validated as affordable and practical enough for everyday use on delivery routes.

During assignment submissions and examination periods, the demand for printing increases, leading to longer waiting times and inconvenience.

INKZY addresses this situation by providing an automated, on-campus printing kiosk that allows students to upload documents, select printing options, make digital payments, and collect their prints conveniently from the kiosk.

problems.title: FPGA road hazard detector
problems.owner: Commuter, commercial and emergency vehicle operators
problems.summary: Detect road hazards and surface type offline, on low-power hardware in the vehicle.

detail.whoYouWorkWith: Two-wheeler commuters, gig delivery workers, rural two-wheeler operators, and community road-safety advocacy groups who navigate poorly illuminated, unpaved, or weather-damaged roadways daily without structural vehicular cabin protection.
detail.situation: Standard navigation apps guide drivers purely on map coordinates without recognizing physical road conditions. Drivers frequently turn onto degraded rural paths, narrow trails, mud tracks, or waterlogged stretches that are completely unsuited for their vehicle's ground clearance, width, or traction limits.
detail.whatIsGoingWrong: A route passable for a tractor or 4x4 SUV causes light delivery vans and ambulances to bottom out or get stuck, passenger cars to scrape underbodies, and two-wheelers to slip. Getting stranded or damaged on remote, unpaved roads leads to delayed emergency responses, disrupted supply chains, vehicle damage, and serious road accidents.
detail.whyNotFixed: Cloud-based AI cannot run in rural dead zones and adds dangerous transmission latency. Meanwhile, existing automotive edge GPUs consume 15W–30W+, which overheats without large cooling systems and rapidly drains vehicle batteries. Microcontrollers are too weak to run computer vision models in real time, leaving vehicles without affordable, on-device terrain awareness.
detail.whatExists: Standard GPS navigation apps, Software-only smartphone dashcam tools and High-end car ADAS systems
detail.whatYouHave:
Hardware Platform: AMD/Xilinx FPGA development board

Development Environment: Vivado Design Suite, Vivado HLS / SystemVerilog toolchain, and PYNQ Python-C drivers.

Datasets & Models: Road surface datasets (tar, gravel, mud, standing water), pothole/hazard bounding-box datasets, and lightweight 2D CNN backbones.

System Budget: Sub-3W on-chip power envelope running on local Block RAM (BRAM) and DSP slices.
detail.findingYourApproach:
1. Train a lightweight multi-task 2D CNN model to perform simultaneous road terrain classification and hazard boundary detection.

2. Build a parameterized Processing Element (PE) systolic array and on-chip line buffer in RTL/HLS to accelerate 2D convolutions with minimal memory overhead.

3. Implement a programmable layer scheduler so the accelerator can run arbitrary CNN layer sizes, strides, and skip connections.

4. Develop a vehicle-profile decision engine that compares detected road surface traction and path limits against selected vehicle types (2-wheeler, 3-wheeler, sedan, delivery van, SUV) to output real-time Safe, Caution, or No-Go warnings.
detail.rules:
1. 100% Offline Operation: Complete vision processing, terrain classification, and vehicle feasibility evaluation must run strictly on-device without internet or cloud communication.

2. Power Cap: Total accelerator hardware power dissipation must stay under 3.0 Watts.

3. Real-Time Performance: Total frame latency must not exceed 30 ms ( ≥ 30 FPS) to alert the driver before entering impassable terrain.

4. Accuracy Retention: Hardware quantization (INT8/FP16/FP8) must maintain accuracy within 2% of the original floating-point model.
detail.doneIn90Days: In 90 days, the team will develop, train, and quantize a multi-task CNN model that classifies road terrains (tar, gravel, mud, water) and detects hazards with over 85% accuracy. A vehicle-matching rule engine will be completed in Python to generate real-time Safe, Caution, or No-Go alerts for different vehicle types. In hardware, a parameterized 2D convolution core will be designed and validated in software simulation (Vivado HLS/xsim) using test vectors exported from the trained model. This delivers a verified AI pipeline and simulation-ready accelerator architecture, establishing the complete foundation for future FPGA board deployment.

problems.title: Learned anomaly detection for rural infrastructure

detail.whatIsGoingWrong: Water leakage, pump malfunction, abnormal electricity consumption, overheating and other unusual conditions can remain unnoticed for long periods because continuous intelligent monitoring is not readily available.
detail.whyNotFixed: Existing systems generally focus on a single parameter or use fixed threshold values. Many solutions can also be expensive or difficult to deploy in resource-limited communities.
